Abstract.

The classical bond lattice of a graph was used in a formula of Whitney to compute the chromatic polynomial. In this paper, we use weighted versions of the bond lattice, to introduce and study a new polynomial and a new symmetric function invariant of a graph. Examples of the new polynomial invariant include the classical Narayana polynomials (for the path graph), the tree-Eulerian polynomials (for the complete graph), and the binomial-Eulerian polynomials (for the star graph). These examples suggest an interesting connection to hh-polynomials of general graph-associahedra. We prove that for any chordal graph, our polynomial graph invariant is γ\gamma-positive.

Multiweighted bond posets yield a symmetric function graph invariant that is an analog of the chromatic polynomial. The highest degree homogeneous component of this symmetric function is of particular interest. The parking function symmetric function introduced by Haiman arises as an example, as do symmetric functions studied by the first author in connection with multibracketed Lie algebras and with colored exterior algebras. The γ\gamma-positivity result mentioned above is a specialization of an ee-positivity result for the highest degree homogeneous component, which we prove for any chordal graph using the theory of lexicographic shellability. We conjecture that this symmetric function is Schur-log-concave, which specializes to Huh’s log-concavity theorem for the chromatic polynomial.

Key words and phrases: 
weighted partitions, bond lattice, chromatic polynomial, graph associahedra, gamma-positivity and unimodality, symmetric functions, lexicographic shellability

1. Introduction

In [8] Björner and Welker introduce the notion of Rees product of posets, which is a combinatorial analog of the Rees construction for semigroup algebras. A particular example that they consider can be viewed as a weighted version of the Boolean algebra ℬn\mathcal{B}_{n}, i.e., the lattice of subsets of the set [n]:={1,2,…,n}[n]:=\{1,2,\dots,n\}. A weighted set BvB^{v} is a finite set BB together with a weight v∈{0,1,…,|B|−1}v\in\{0,1,\dots,|B|-1\} attached (the empty set does not get any weight). The weighted Boolean algebra 𝒲​ℬn\mathcal{WB}_{n} consists of the weighted subsets of [n][n] with a certain order relation that reduces to the usual inclusion order on subsets when the weights are ignored.

The poset 𝒲​ℬn\mathcal{WB}_{n} is pure (or graded) of length nn, but is not bounded. Its minimum element is

0^=∅\hat{0}=\emptyset

and its maximal elements are

[n]0,[n]1,…,[n]n−1.[n]^{0},[n]^{1},\dots,[n]^{n-1}.

The Hasse diagram of 𝒲​ℬ3\mathcal{WB}_{3} is shown in Figure 1.1, where the commas and the set brackets have been omitted.

Shareshian and Wachs [37] prove that 𝒲​ℬn∪{1^}\mathcal{WB}_{n}\cup\{\hat{1}\}, where 1^\hat{1} is an attached maximum element, is EL-shellable and that the classical Eulerian polynomial An​(t)A_{n}(t) arises when one applies the Möbius function μ𝒲​ℬn\mu_{\mathcal{WB}_{n}} to the maximal intervals of 𝒲​ℬn{\mathcal{WB}_{n}}. More precisely they prove

(1.1) (−1)n​∑j=0n−1μ𝒲​ℬn​(0^,[n]j)​tj=An​(t):=∑σ∈𝔖ntdes(σ),(-1)^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mu_{\mathcal{WB}_{n}}(\hat{0},[n]^{j})\,t^{j}=A_{n}(t):=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(\sigma)},

where 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} is the symmetric group on [n][n] and des\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits is the descent statistic defined by

des(σ):=|{i∈[n−1]:σ⁡(i)>σ⁡(i+1)}|.\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(\sigma):=|\{i\in[n-1]:\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)\}|.

A weighted version of the partition lattice Πn\Pi_{n}, analogous to the weighted Boolean algebra 𝒲​ℬn\mathcal{WB}_{n}, was proposed by Dotsenko and Khoroshkin in [13] as a tool for studying the free Lie algebra with two compatible brackets. In [20] González D’León and Wachs carry out a study of this poset and its connection to the free Lie algebra with two compatible brackets.

A weighted partition of [n][n] is a set {B1v1,B2v2,…,Btvt}\{B_{1}^{v_{1}},B_{2}^{v_{2}},...,B_{t}^{v_{t}}\} where

  • •

    {B1,B2,…,Bt}\{B_{1},B_{2},...,B_{t}\} is a partition of [n][n]

  • •

    each BiviB_{i}^{v_{i}} is a weighted set, i.e., vi∈{0,1,2,…,|Bi|−1}v_{i}\in\{0,1,2,...,|B_{i}|-1\} for all ii.

The poset of weighted partitions 𝒲​Πn\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n} is the set of weighted partitions of [n][n] with a certain order relation that reduces to the usual refinement order on partitions when the weights are ignored.11 1 Precise definitions are given in Section 2.22 2 The notation 𝒲​Πn\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n} used in this paper is different from that of [20] where the notation Πnw\Pi_{n}^{w} is used instead. The poset 𝒲​Πn\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n} is pure of length n−1n-1, but is not bounded. Its minimum element is

(1.2) 0^:={{1}0,{2}0,…,{n}0}\hat{0}:=\{\{1\}^{0},\{2\}^{0},\dots,\{n\}^{0}\}

and it has nn maximal elements

(1.3) {[n]0},{[n]1},…,{[n]n−1}.\{[n]^{0}\},\,\{[n]^{1}\},\dots,\{[n]^{n-1}\}.

As is customary for ordinary partitions, we sometimes use the notation B1v1|B2v2​|⋯|​BkvkB_{1}^{v_{1}}|B_{2}^{v_{2}}|\cdots|B_{k}^{v_{k}} with set brackets omitted to denote the weighted partition {B1v1,…,Bkvk}\{B_{1}^{v_{1}},\dots,B_{k}^{v_{k}}\}. The Hasse diagram of 𝒲​Π3\mathcal{W}\Pi_{3} is shown in Figure 1.2.

In [20] González D’León and Wachs prove that 𝒲​Πn∪{1^}\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n}\cup\{\hat{1}\} is EL-shellable and that the tree-Eulerian polynomial (cf. [21]), studied by Gessel and Seo [18, Theorem 9.1], arises when one applies the Möbius function μ𝒲​Πn\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n}} to the maximal intervals of 𝒲​Πn{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n}}. More precisely, they prove

∑j=0n−1μ𝒲​Πn​(0^,{[n]j})​tj=(−1)n−1​∑T∈𝒯ntdes(T),\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n}}(\hat{0},\{[n]^{j}\})\,t^{j}=(-1)^{n-1}\sum_{T\in\mathcal{T}_{n}}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(T)},

where 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} is the set of (nonplanar) rooted trees on node set [n][n] and des(T)\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(T) is the descent statistic on T∈𝒯nT\in\mathcal{T}_{n} that gives the number of pairs (p,c)(p,c) for which pp is the parent of cc in TT and p>cp>c.

In this paper we introduce a weighted version of the bond lattice of a graph, which generalizes the weighted partition poset. The bond lattice ΠG\Pi_{G} of a graph GG on vertex set [n][n] is the induced subposet of Πn\Pi_{n} consisting of the partitions whose blocks induce connected subgraphs of GG. For the path graph P3=([3],{{1,2},{2,3}})P_{3}=([3],\{\{1,2\},\{2,3\}\}), the Hasse diagram of ΠP3\Pi_{P_{3}} is given in Figure 1.3. Note that the partition 13|213|2 does not belong to ΠP3\Pi_{P_{3}} since the induced subgraph P3|{1,3}P_{3}|_{\{1,3\}} is not connected.

Bond lattices play an important role in the study of chromatic polynomials. Indeed, a formula of Whitney [47] for the chromatic polynomial χG​(t)\chi_{G}(t) of GG is given by

(1.4) χG​(t)=∑π∈ΠGμΠG​(0^,π)​t|π|.\chi_{G}(t)=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{G}}\mu_{\Pi_{G}}(\hat{0},\pi)t^{|\pi|}.

Through the weighted version of the bond lattice, we introduce and study a different polynomial graph invariant.

Let GG be a graph on vertex set [n][n]. We define the weighted bond poset 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G} of GG to be the induced subposet of 𝒲​Πn\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n} consisting of weighted partitions 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi} whose underlying partitions π\pi are in ΠG\Pi_{G}. Note that for the complete graph KnK_{n}, we have

𝒲​ΠKn=𝒲​Πn.\mathcal{W}\Pi_{K_{n}}=\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n}.

The weighted bond poset 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G} is pure, but not bounded. Its minimum element is the same as that for 𝒲​Πn\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n}, given in (1.2). If GG is connected, its maximal elements are also the same as those for 𝒲​Πn\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n}, which are given in (1.3). For the path graph P3P_{3}, the Hasse diagram of 𝒲​ΠP3\mathcal{W}\Pi_{P_{3}} is given in Figure 1.4.

Now let GG be a connected graph on vertex set [n][n] and define the Möbius polynomial of GG to be

μG​(t):=∑j=0n−1μ𝒲​ΠG​(0^,{[n]j})​tj.\mu_{G}(t):=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}}(\hat{0},\{[n]^{j}\})t^{j}.

For graphs GG that are not connected, the sum is taken over the maximal elements of 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}. The constant term μG​(0)\mu_{G}(0) is the Möbius invariant μ⁡(ΠG)\mu(\Pi_{G}) of the bond poset ΠG\Pi_{G}. From Figures 1.2 and 1.4, we see that

(1.5) μK3​(t)=2+5​t+2​t2​ and ​μP3​(t)=1+3​t+t2.\mu_{K_{3}}(t)=2+5t+2t^{2}\,\,\mbox{ and }\,\,\mu_{P_{3}}(t)=1+3t+t^{2}.

We show that if GG is a path graph on [n][n] then (−1)n−1​μG​(t)(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{G}(t) is a Narayana polynomial and if GG is the star graph on [n][n] then (−1)n−1​μG​(t)(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{G}(t) is a polynomial arising in the work of Postnikov, Reiner, and Williams [34] on graph associahedra, called the binomial-Eulerian polynomial in [38].33 3 Definitions are given in Sections 3.2 and 3.3. As was discussed in [34], the Narayana polynomials and the binomial-Eulerian polynomials are hh-polynomials of certain graph associahedra. The Möbius polynomials of these examples motivated the following conjecture, which appeared in an earlier version of this paper and has since been proved by Avila, Carrillo, and the first author [3, 2].

Conjecture 1.1.

Let GG be a graph with nn vertices and kk connected components. Let 𝒫G\mathcal{P}_{G} be the graph associahedron associated with GG and let h𝒫G​(t)h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t) denote its hh-polynomial. Then

(−1)n−k​μG​(t)−h𝒫G​(t)⪰0,(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t)\succeq 0,

with equality if GG is a forest, where p⁡(t)⪰0p(t)\succeq 0 indicates that all the coefficients of the polynomial p⁡(t)p(t) are nonnegative.

In [34] Postnikov, Reiner, and Williams establish the important γ\gamma-positivity property for hAG​(t)h_{\mathcal{\mathcal{}}A_{G}}(t) when GG is a chordal graph in order to confirm, for this particular class of polytopes, a well known conjecture of Gal [17], which asserts that every simple flag polytope is γ\gamma-positive. The γ\gamma-positivity property implies unimodality (and palindromicity), which was established by Stanley [40] for all convex polytopes. In this paper we prove the analogous result for μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t).

Theorem 1.2.

If GG is a chordal graph with nn vertices and kk connected components then (−1)n−k​μG​(t)(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t) is γ\gamma-positive.

Our proof of Theorem 1.2 relies on an EL-labeling of the weighted bond poset of a chordal graph and the theory of lexicographic shellability. Previously this technique was used in [37, 32, 23] to establish γ\gamma-positivity of variations and generalizations of (−1)n​∑j=0nμ𝒲​ℬn​(0^,[n]j)​tj(-1)^{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\mu_{\mathcal{WB}_{n}}(\hat{0},[n]^{j})t^{j} and in [20] to establish γ\gamma-positivity of (−1)n−1​μKn​(t)(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{K_{n}}(t).

Our results hold in greater generality. In [22] González D’León considers a multiweighted generalization of the weighted partition poset 𝒲​Πn\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n} in order to study the multilinear component of the free Lie algebra with more than two compatible brackets. In [23] he also introduces a multiweighted generalization of a variant of the weighted Boolean algebra 𝒲​ℬn\mathcal{WB}_{n} in order to study the multilinear component of colored exterior algebras. In this paper we consider an analogous multiweighted generalization of the weighted bond posets 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}. This yields a symmetric function generalization MG​(𝐱)M_{G}(\mathbf{x}) of the Möbius polynomial μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t), which we call the Möbius symmetric function of GG. Indeed, the specialization MG​(𝐱)​(1,t,0,…)M_{G}(\mathbf{x})(1,t,0,\dots) yields μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t). The specialization MG​(𝐱)​(1,0,0,…)=μG​(0)M_{G}(\mathbf{x})(1,0,0,\dots)=\mu_{G}(0) yields the Möbius invariant μ⁡(ΠG)\mu(\Pi_{G}).

When GG is the complete graph KnK_{n}, we have that (−1)n−1​MG​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-1}M_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is equal to the symmetric function studied in [22], whose coefficients give the dimensions of components of the free Lie algebra with multiple compatible brackets. When GG is the star graph with nn vertices, (−1)n−1​MG​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-1}M_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is equal to the symmetric function studied in [23], whose coefficients give the dimensions of components of the colored exterior algebra. We show that when GG is equal to the path graph with nn vertices, (−1)n−1​ω​MG​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-1}\omega M_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is the parking function symmetric function of Haiman [28], where ω\omega is the standard involution on the ring of symmetric functions taking the complete homogeneous symmetric function hnh_{n} to the elementary symmetric function ene_{n}.

We also obtain a multiweighted generalization of Theorem 1.2 whose proof relies on an EL-labeling of the multiweighted bond poset of a chordal graph.

Theorem 1.3.

If GG is a chordal graph with nn vertices and kk connected components then the symmetric function (−1)n−k​MG​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-k}M_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is ee-positive, in the sense that when expanded in the basis of elementary symmetric functions {eλ:λ⊢n−1}\{e_{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n-1\}, the coefficients are nonnegative.

We conjecture that Theorem 1.3 is true for all graphs.

A symmetric function generalization of the chromatic polynomial can also be obtained from the multiweighted bond posets. The maximal degree component of this symmetric function is MG​(𝐱)M_{G}(\mathbf{x}). For chordal graphs GG, we establish a property that we call alternating ee-positivity and we conjecture that it holds for all graphs. We also present a conjecture asserting that this symmetric function has a property that we call Schur-log-concavity. This conjecture generalizes Huh’s celebrated log-concavity result for the chromatic polynomial [31].

The paper is organized as follows. Sections 2 - 4 deal with the Möbius polynomial μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) and Sections 5 -  7 deal with the symmetric function generalizations of the Möbius polynomial and the chromatic polynomial.

In Section 2, we present the definitions and basic properties of the weighted bond lattice and Möbius polynomial of a graph. In Section 3, we present recurrence relations which enable us to show that (−1)n−1​μG​(t)(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{G}(t) is the tree-Eulerian polynomial when GG is the complete graph, the Narayana polynomial when GG is the path graph, and the binomial-Eulerian polynomial when GG is the star graph. We also discuss in Section 3 the connection with graph associahedra. In Section 4, we present γ\gamma-positivity results for Möbius polynomials of chordal graphs, which are analogous to those of Postnikov, Reiner and Williams [34] for hh-polynomials of graph associahedra of chordal graphs. Proofs of some of the results in Sections 3 and 4 are deferred to Sections 5 and 6 where more general results are proved.

In Section 5, we introduce the multiweighted generalization of the weighted bond poset and establish recurrence relations for the Möbius symmetric functions, which enable us to derive the relationship between the Möbius symmetric function of the path graph and the parking function symmetric function. Section 6 deals with EL-shellability of the multiweighted bond poset and its ee-positivity implications, which include Theorem 1.3. The symmetric function generalization of the chromatic polynomial is discussed in Section 7.

2. Definitions and basic properties

Let ΠS\Pi_{S} denote the lattice of partitions of the finite set SS partially ordered by refinement, that is π≤π′\pi\leq\pi^{\prime} in ΠS\Pi_{S} if blocks of π\pi are merged to obtain blocks of π′\pi^{\prime}. See [43] for basic information, terminology and notation on partially ordered sets.

A weighted partition of a set SS is a set 𝝅={B1v1,B2v2,…,Bkvk}\boldsymbol{\pi}=\{B_{1}^{v_{1}},B_{2}^{v_{2}},...,B_{k}^{v_{k}}\} of weighted blocks such that {B1,B2,…,Bk}\{B_{1},B_{2},...,B_{k}\} is a partition of SS and vi∈{0,1,2,…,|Bi|−1}v_{i}\in\{0,1,2,...,|B_{i}|-1\} for all i∈[k]i\in[k]. We refer to π={B1,B2,…,Bk}\pi=\{B_{1},B_{2},...,B_{k}\} as the underlying partition of 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi} and viv_{i} as the weight of the block BiB_{i}. The poset of weighted partitions 𝒲​ΠS\mathcal{W}\Pi_{S} is the set of weighted partitions of SS with order relation given by

{A1w1,A2w2,…,Ajwj}≤{B1v1,B2v2,…,Bkvk}\{A_{1}^{w_{1}},A_{2}^{w_{2}},...,A_{j}^{w_{j}}\}\leq\{B_{1}^{v_{1}},B_{2}^{v_{2}},...,B_{k}^{v_{k}}\}

if the following conditions hold:

  • •

    {A1,A2,…,Aj}≤{B1,B2,…,Bk}\{A_{1},A_{2},...,A_{j}\}\leq\{B_{1},B_{2},...,B_{k}\} in ΠS\Pi_{S}

  • •

    if Bm=Ai1∪Ai2∪…∪AilB_{m}=A_{i_{1}}\cup A_{i_{2}}\cup...\cup A_{i_{l}} then vm−(wi1+wi2+…+wil)∈{0,1,…,l−1}v_{m}-(w_{i_{1}}+w_{i_{2}}+...+w_{i_{l}})\in\{0,1,...,l-1\}.

Equivalently, the covering relation ⋖\lessdot is given by

{A1w1,A2w2,…,Ajwj}⋖{B1v1,B2v2,…,Bkvk}\{A_{1}^{w_{1}},A_{2}^{w_{2}},...,A_{j}^{w_{j}}\}\lessdot\{B_{1}^{v_{1}},B_{2}^{v_{2}},...,B_{k}^{v_{k}}\}

if the following conditions hold:

  • •

    {A1,A2,…,Aj}⋖{B1,B2,…,Bk}\{A_{1},A_{2},\dots,A_{j}\}\lessdot\{B_{1},B_{2},\dots,B_{k}\} in ΠS\Pi_{S}

  • •

    if Bm=Ah∪AiB_{m}=A_{h}\cup A_{i}, where h≠ih\neq i, then vm−(wh+wi)∈{0,1}v_{m}-(w_{h}+w_{i})\in\{0,1\}

  • •

    if Bm=AiB_{m}=A_{i} then vm=wiv_{m}=w_{i}.

For each n∈ℤ>0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, let Πn:=Π[n]\Pi_{n}:=\Pi_{[n]} and 𝒲​Πn:=𝒲​Π[n]\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n}:=\mathcal{W}\Pi_{[n]}, where [n]:={1,2,…,n}[n]:=\{1,2,\dots,n\}. Recall that the Hasse diagram of 𝒲​Π3\mathcal{W}\Pi_{3} (using the notation B1w1|B2w2|,…,|BkwkB_{1}^{w_{1}}|B_{2}^{w_{2}}|,\dots,|B_{k}^{w_{k}} with set brackets omitted to denote the weighted partition {B1w1,…,Bkwk}\{B_{1}^{w_{1}},\dots,B_{k}^{w_{k}}\}) is given in Figure 1.2.

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a finite graph. The bond lattice ΠG\Pi_{G} of GG is the induced subposet of ΠV\Pi_{V} consisting of the partitions of VV whose blocks induce connected subgraphs of GG. The weighted bond poset 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G} of GG is defined to be the induced subposet of 𝒲​ΠV\mathcal{W}\Pi_{V} consisting of all weighted partitions whose underlying partitions are in ΠG\Pi_{G}. Recall that the Hasse diagrams of ΠP3\Pi_{P_{3}} and 𝒲​ΠP3\mathcal{W}\Pi_{P_{3}} are given in Figure 1.3 and 1.4, respectively.

Let KnK_{n} be the complete graph on vertex set [n][n]. Since

𝒲​ΠKn=𝒲​Πn,\mathcal{W}\Pi_{K_{n}}=\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n},

the weighted bond poset of a graph is a more general structure than the weighted partition poset.

For 𝜶≤𝜷\boldsymbol{\alpha}\leq\boldsymbol{\beta} in 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}, let

[𝜶,𝜷]G={𝝅∈𝒲​ΠG:𝜶≤𝝅≤𝜷}.[\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}]_{G}=\{\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}:\boldsymbol{\alpha}\leq\boldsymbol{\pi}\leq\boldsymbol{\beta}\}.

When G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is connected, for convenience, we will drop the set brackets for the maximal elements of 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}. That is, we write the weighted partition {Vw}\{V^{w}\} as VwV^{w} and the maximal interval [0^,{Vw}]G[\hat{0},\{V^{w}\}]_{G} as [0^,Vw]G[\hat{0},V^{w}]_{G}

A poset is said to be bounded if it has a minimum element, which is denoted 0^\hat{0}, and a maximum element, which is denoted 1^\hat{1}. A poset is said to be pure (or graded) if all its maximal chains have the same length, where the length of a chain is one less than the number of elements in the chain. The length ℓ⁡(P)\ell(P) of a pure poset PP is the common length of its maximal chains.

The bond lattice ΠG\Pi_{G} of any connected graph GG is pure and bounded, while the weighted bond poset 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G} is pure but not bounded even when GG is connected. Indeed if V={v1,v2,…,vn}V=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{n}\} then 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G} has minimum element

0^:={{v1}0,{v2}0,…,{vn}0}\hat{0}:=\{\{v_{1}\}^{0},\{v_{2}\}^{0},\dots,\{v_{n}\}^{0}\}

and if GG is connected, 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G} it has nn maximal elements

V0,V1,…,Vn−1,V^{0},\,V^{1},\dots,V^{n-1},

but no maximum element unless n=1n=1. If G=(V,E)G=(V,E) has connected components Gi=(Vi,Ei)G_{i}=(V_{i},E_{i}), where i∈[k]i\in[k], then the maximal elements of 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G} are all the weighted partitions whose underlying partition is {V1,…,Vk}\{V_{1},\dots,V_{k}\}. Note that

ℓ⁡(𝒲​ΠG)=ℓ⁡(ΠG)=|V|−k.\ell(\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G})=\ell(\Pi_{G})=|V|-k.

We have the following observation whose straightforward proof is left to the reader.

Proposition 2.1.

Let GG be a graph whose connected components are G1,…,GkG_{1},\dots,G_{k}. Then the map

φ:𝒲ΠG1×⋯×𝒲ΠGk→𝒲ΠG\varphi:\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G_{1}}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G_{k}}\to\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}

defined by φ⁡(𝛑1,…,𝛑k)=𝛑1∪⋯∪𝛑k\varphi(\boldsymbol{\pi}_{1},\dots,\boldsymbol{\pi}_{k})=\boldsymbol{\pi}_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\boldsymbol{\pi}_{k} is a poset isomorphism.

Recall that the Möbius function of a poset PP is defined recursively on intervals [x,y][x,y] of PP by

(2.1) μP​(x,y)={1if ​x=y,−∑x≤z<yμP(x,z)if ​x<y.\mu_{P}(x,y)=\begin{cases}1&\mbox{if }x=y,\\ -\displaystyle\sum_{x\leq z<y}\mu_{P}(x,z)&\mbox{if }x<y.\end{cases}

Define the Möbius polynomial of a graph GG by

μG​(t):=∑𝝅∈Max(𝒲​ΠG)μ𝒲​ΠG​(0^,𝝅)​tw⁡(𝝅),\mu_{G}(t):=\sum_{\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\mathop{\rm Max}\nolimits(\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G})}\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}}(\hat{0},\boldsymbol{\pi})t^{w(\boldsymbol{\pi})},

where Max(P)\mathop{\rm Max}\nolimits(P) is the set of maximal elements of a poset PP, and w⁡(𝝅)w(\boldsymbol{\pi}) is the sum of the weights of the blocks of 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi} for any weighted partition 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi}. If GG is a connected graph on vertex set VV then

(2.2) μG​(t)=∑j=0|V|−1μ𝒲​ΠG​(0^,Vj)​tj.\mu_{G}(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{|V|-1}\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}}(\hat{0},V^{j})\,t^{j}.

The following proposition, which is a consequence of Proposition 2.1 and of the multiplicative property of the Möbius function (see [43, Proposition 3.8.2]) tells us that we can focus on Möbius polynomials of connected graphs.

Proposition 2.2.

Let GG be a graph whose connected components are G1,…,GkG_{1},\dots,G_{k}. Then

μG​(t)=∏i=1kμGi​(t).\mu_{G}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{G_{i}}(t).
Proof.

For each i∈[k]i\in[k], let ViV_{i} be the vertex set of GiG_{i}. The maximal elements of 𝒲​ΠG\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G} are of the form {V1j1,V2j2,…,Vkjk}\{V_{1}^{j_{1}},V_{2}^{j_{2}},\dots,V_{k}^{j_{k}}\}, where 0≤ji≤|Vi|−10\leq j_{i}\leq|V_{i}|-1 for each ii. It follows that

μG​(t)=∑j1=0|V1|−1∑j2=0|V2|−1…​∑jk=0|Vk|−1μ𝒲​ΠG​(0^,{V1j1,V2j2,…,Vkjk})​tj1+j2+⋯+jk.\mu_{G}(t)=\sum_{j_{1}=0}^{|V_{1}|-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0}^{|V_{2}|-1}\dots\sum_{j_{k}=0}^{|V_{k}|-1}\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}}(\hat{0},\{V_{1}^{j_{1}},V_{2}^{j_{2}},\dots,V_{k}^{j_{k}}\})t^{j_{1}+j_{2}+\dots+j_{k}}.

By Proposition 2.1

μ𝒲​ΠG(0^,{V1j1,…,Vkjk})=μ×i=1k𝒲ΠGi((0^1,⋯,0^k),({V1j1},…,{Vkjk})),\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}}(\hat{0},\{V_{1}^{j_{1}},\dots,V_{k}^{j_{k}}\})=\mu_{\times_{i=1}^{k}\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G_{i}}}((\hat{0}_{1},\cdots,\hat{0}_{k}),(\{V_{1}^{j_{1}}\},\dots,\{V_{k}^{j_{k}}\})),

where 0^i\hat{0}_{i} is the minimum element of 𝒲​ΠGi\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G_{i}}. Now by the multiplicative property of the Möbius function (see [43, Proposition 3.8.2]),

μ×i=1k𝒲ΠGi((0^1,⋯,0^k),({V1j1},…,{Vkjk}))=∏i=1kμ𝒲​ΠGi(0^i,{Viji}).\mu_{\times_{i=1}^{k}\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G_{i}}}((\hat{0}_{1},\cdots,\hat{0}_{k}),(\{V_{1}^{j_{1}}\},\dots,\{V_{k}^{j_{k}}\}))=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G_{i}}}(\hat{0}_{i},\{V_{i}^{j_{i}}\}).

Putting these equations together yields,

μG​(t)\displaystyle\mu_{G}(t) =∑j1=0|V1|−1∑j2=0|V2|−1…​∑jk=0|Vk|−1(∏i=1kμ𝒲​ΠGi​(0^i,{Viji}))​tj1+j2+⋯+jk\displaystyle=\sum_{j_{1}=0}^{|V_{1}|-1}\sum_{j_{2}=0}^{|V_{2}|-1}\dots\sum_{j_{k}=0}^{|V_{k}|-1}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G_{i}}}(\hat{0}_{i},\{V_{i}^{j_{i}}\})\right)t^{j_{1}+j_{2}+\dots+j_{k}}
=∏i=1k∑ji=0|Vi|−1μ𝒲​ΠGi​(0^,Viji)​tji\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\sum_{j_{i}=0}^{|V_{i}|-1}\mu_{\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G_{i}}}(\hat{0},V_{i}^{j_{i}})t^{j_{i}}
=∏i=1kμGi​(t).∎\displaystyle=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{G_{i}}(t).\qed
Proposition 2.3.

Let GG be a connected graph on vertex set VV. Then for all j=0,…,|V|−1j=0,\dots,|V|-1,

[0^,Vj]G≅[0^,V|V|−1−j]G,[\hat{0},V^{j}]_{G}\cong[\hat{0},V^{|V|-1-j}]_{G},

and both intervals [0^,V0]G[\hat{0},V^{0}]_{G} and [0^,V|V|−1]G[\hat{0},V^{|V|-1}]_{G} are isomorphic to the bond lattice ΠG\Pi_{G}.

Proof.

It is not difficult to see that the map from [0^,Vj]G[\hat{0},V^{j}]_{G} to [0^,V|V|−1−j]G[\hat{0},V^{|V|-1-j}]_{G} which takes {B1w1,…,Bkwk}\{B_{1}^{w_{1}},\dots,B_{k}^{w_{k}}\} to {B1|B1|−1−w1,…,Bk|Bk|−1−wk}\{B_{1}^{|B_{1}|-1-w_{1}},\dots,B_{k}^{|B_{k}|-1-w_{k}}\} is a well-defined poset isomorphism. Since all the blocks of the weighted partitions in [0^,V0]G[\hat{0},V^{0}]_{G} have weight 00, the map that removes these weights is an isomorphism from [0^,V0]G[\hat{0},V^{0}]_{G} to ΠG\Pi_{G}. ∎

Proposition 2.4.

Let GG be a graph with nn vertices and kk connected components. Then

  1. (1)

    μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) has degree n−kn-k.

  2. (2)

    μG​(0)\mu_{G}(0) is equal to the Möbius invariant μ⁡(ΠG)\mu(\Pi_{G}) of the bond lattice ΠG\Pi_{G}.

  3. (3)

    μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) is palindromic in the sense that the coefficient of tjt^{j} equals the coefficient of tn−k−jt^{n-k-j} for all j=0,…,n−kj=0,\dots,n-k.

Proof.

Item (1) for connected graphs follows from Equation (2.2), Proposition 2.3, and the fact that the Möbius invariant of a geometric lattice is never 00; see [43, Exercise 3.100b]. Indeed, by (2.2), the degree of μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) is at most n−1n-1 and by Proposition 2.3, the coefficient of tn−1t^{n-1} is μ⁡(ΠG)\mu(\Pi_{G}). Thus since ΠG\Pi_{G} is a geometric lattice, the coefficient of tn−1t^{n-1} is not 00. For graphs that are not connected, item (1) follows from the connected case and Proposition 2.2.

Item (2) for connected graphs follows from Proposition 2.3. To prove item (2) in general, we first note that Proposition 2.2 implies that μG​(0)=∏i=1kμGi​(0)\mu_{G}(0)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{G_{i}}(0), where the GiG_{i} are the connected components of GG. Since ΠG≅ΠG1×⋯×ΠGk\Pi_{G}\cong\Pi_{G_{1}}\times\cdots\times\Pi_{G_{k}}, item (2) now follows from the multiplicative property of the Möbius invariant and the connected case.

To prove item (3), we use Propositions 2.2 and 2.3 and the fact that products of palindromic polynomials are palindromic. ∎

3. Recurrence relations and examples

We present recurrence relations for the Möbius polynomials, which can be used to study specific examples.

3.1. Recurrence relations for the Möbius polynomials

Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E). For B⊆VB\subseteq V, the restriction G|BG|_{B} is defined to be the subgraph of GG induced by the vertex set BB. For π∈ΠG\pi\in\Pi_{G}, the contraction G/πG/\pi is defined to be the graph whose vertices are the blocks of π\pi and whose edge set is

{{A,B}⊆π∣A≠B,{a,b}∈E for some a∈A and b∈B}.\{\{A,B\}\subseteq\pi\mid A\neq B,\,\{a,b\}\in E\text{ for some }a\in A\text{ and }b\in B\}.

Note that if π∈ΠG\pi\in\Pi_{G} then the restriction G|BG|_{B} is connected for all B∈πB\in\pi and the contraction G/πG/\pi is connected if and only if GG is connected.

Although the following result can be proved directly by simply using the recursive definition of Möbius function for the first recurrence relation (3.1) and the dual version of the definition of Möbius function for the second recurrence relation (3.2), we prove it as a special case of Theorem 5.7 below.

Theorem 3.1.

Let GG be a connected graph with more than one vertex. Then μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) can be computed recursively by either

(3.1) μG(t)=−∑π∈ΠG∖{1^}[|π|]t∏B∈πμG|B(t),\displaystyle\mu_{G}(t)=-\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{G}\setminus\{\hat{1}\}}[|\pi|]_{t}\prod_{B\in\pi}\mu_{G|_{B}}(t),

or

(3.2) μG(t)=−∑π∈ΠG∖{0^}μG/π(t)∏B∈π[|B|]t,\displaystyle\mu_{G}(t)=-\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{G}\setminus\{\hat{0}\}}\mu_{G/\pi}(t)\prod_{B\in\pi}[|B|]_{t},

where [k]t:=1+t+⋯+tk−1[k]_{t}:=1+t+\cdots+t^{k-1} is the tt-analog of kk and the initial condition is given by μG​(t)=1\mu_{G}(t)=1 when G=({∙},∅)G=(\{\bullet\},\emptyset), is the graph with one vertex.

The recurrence relation (3.2) in the case of the complete graph

Kn:=([n],{{i,j}:1≤i<j<n})K_{n}:=\left([n],\{\{i,j\}:1\leq i<j<n\}\right)

and the compositional formula (see [42, Theorem 5.1.4]) were used in [20] to obtain the exponential generating function formula

(3.3) ∑n≥1μKn​(t)​ynn!=(∑n≥1[n]t​ynn!)⟨−1⟩=(et​y−eyt−1)⟨−1⟩,\sum_{n\geq 1}\mu_{K_{n}}(t)\dfrac{y^{n}}{n!}=\left(\sum_{n\geq 1}[n]_{t}\dfrac{y^{n}}{n!}\right)^{\langle-1\rangle}=\left(\frac{e^{ty}-e^{y}}{t-1}\right)^{\langle-1\rangle},

where (∙)⟨−1⟩(\bullet)^{\langle-1\rangle} denotes the inverse with respect to composition (substitution) of power series. This and [14, Equation (10)] were used in [20] to obtain the formula,

(3.4) (−1)n−1​μKn​(t)=∏i=1n−1((n−i)+i​t).(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{K_{n}}(t)=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}((n-i)+it).

A nice consequence of this formula is

(−1)n−1​μKn​(1)=nn−1,(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{K_{n}}(1)=n^{n-1},

which by Cayley’s formula is the number of (nonplanar) rooted trees on node set [n][n]. Equation 3.4 and a refinement of Cayley’s formula obtained by Gessel and Seo [18, Theorem 9.1] yield

(3.5) (−1)n−1​μKn​(t)=∑T∈𝒯ntdes(T),(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{K_{n}}(t)=\sum_{T\in\mathcal{T}_{n}}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(T)},

where 𝒯n\mathcal{T}_{n} is the set of (nonplanar) rooted trees on node set [n][n] and des(T)\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(T) is the number of pairs (p,c)(p,c), where pp is the parent of cc in TT and p>cp>c. We call the polynomial on the right hand side of (3.5), the tree-Eulerian polynomial; cf. [21].

3.2. The path graph and Narayana polynomials

Define the path graph to be

Pn:=([n],{{i,i+1}:i∈[n−1]}).P_{n}:=([n],\{\{i,i+1\}:i\in[n-1]\}).

In this section, we apply the recurrence relations of Theorem 3.1 to the path graphs to show that the signless Möbius polynomials for these graphs are equal to the well known Narayana polynomials.

The Narayana numbers are defined by

(3.6) N⁡(n,j):=1n​(nj)​(nj+1)N(n,j):=\frac{1}{n}\binom{n}{j}\binom{n}{j+1}

and the Narayana polynomials by

Nn​(t):=∑j=0n−1N⁡(n,j)​tj.N_{n}(t):=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}N(n,j)t^{j}.

The Narayana numbers refine the Catalan numbers

Cn:=1n+1​(2​nn).C_{n}:=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}.

Indeed, by Vandermonde’s identity

Nn​(1)=Cn.N_{n}(1)=C_{n}.
Theorem 3.2.

For n≥1n\geq 1,

(−1)n−1​μPn​(t)=Nn​(t).(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{P_{n}}(t)=N_{n}(t).

Consequently,

(−1)n−1​μPn​(1)=Cn.(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{P_{n}}(1)=C_{n}.
Proof.

The recurrence relations of Theorem 3.1 applied to G=PnG=P_{n} can be expressed as

∑k=1n[k]t​∑(n1,…,nk)⊨n∏i=1kμPni​(t)=δn,1\sum_{k=1}^{n}[k]_{t}\sum_{(n_{1},\dots,n_{k})\vDash n}\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{P_{n_{i}}}(t)=\delta_{n,1}

and

∑k=1nμPk​(t)​∑(n1,…,nk)⊨n∏i=1k[ni]t=δn,1,\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mu_{P_{k}}(t)\sum_{(n_{1},\dots,n_{k})\vDash n}\prod_{i=1}^{k}[n_{i}]_{t}=\delta_{n,1},

where ⊨\vDash denotes “is a composition of”. Both equations are equivalent to the generating function formula

(3.7) ∑n≥1(−1)n−1​μPn​(t)​yn=(∑n≥1(−1)n−1​[n]t​yn)⟨−1⟩=(y(1+y)​(1+t​y))⟨−1⟩,\sum_{n\geq 1}(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{P_{n}}(t)y^{n}=\left(\sum_{n\geq 1}(-1)^{n-1}[n]_{t}\,y^{n}\right)^{\left\langle-1\right\rangle}=\left(\frac{y}{(1+y)(1+ty)}\right)^{\left\langle-1\right\rangle},

where again (∙)⟨−1⟩(\bullet)^{\langle-1\rangle} denotes the compositional inverse.44 4 It is known that y(1+y)​(1+t​y)\frac{y}{(1+y)(1+ty)} is the compositional inverse of the generating function for the Narayana polynomials. For the sake of completeness we are including this proof. Hence, by the Lagrange inversion formula (see [42, Theorem 5.4.2]), n​(−1)n−1​μPn​(t)n(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{P_{n}}(t) is equal to the coefficient of yn−1y^{n-1} in ((1+y)​(1+t​y))n((1+y)(1+ty))^{n}. Since

((1+y)​(1+t​y))n\displaystyle((1+y)(1+ty))^{n} =∑j=0n(nj)​yj​∑j=0n(nj)​(t​y)j\displaystyle=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}y^{j}\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom{n}{j}(ty)^{j}
=∑k≥0(∑j=0k(nj)​(nk−j)​tj)​yk,\displaystyle=\sum_{k\geq 0}\left(\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{n}{j}\binom{n}{k-j}t^{j}\right)y^{k},

the coefficient of yn−1y^{n-1} is

∑j=0n−1(nj)​(nn−1−j)​tj=∑j=0n−1(nj)​(nj+1)​tj.\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n}{j}\binom{n}{n-1-j}t^{j}=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n}{j}\binom{n}{j+1}t^{j}.

This means that

(−1)n−1​μPn​(t)=1n​∑j=0n−1(nj)​(nj+1)​tj,(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{P_{n}}(t)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n}{j}\binom{n}{j+1}t^{j},

which by (3.6) yields the desired result. ∎

3.3. The star graph and binomial-Eulerian polynomials

Define the star graph to be

S​tn:=([n],{{1,i}:i∈{2,…,n}}).St_{n}:=([n],\{\{1,i\}:i\in\{2,\dots,n\}\}).

In this section, we use the recurrence relations of Theorem 3.1 applied to the star graphs to show that the signless Möbius polynomials for these graphs are equal to a variant of the Eulerian polynomials.

Recall that the classical Eulerian polynomials are defined by

(3.8) An​(t):=∑σ∈𝔖ntdes(σ),A_{n}(t):=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(\sigma)},

where

des(σ):=|{i∈[n−1]:σ⁡(i)>σ⁡(i+1)}|.\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(\sigma):=|\{i\in[n-1]:\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)\}|.

Following [38], we refer to the polynomial

A~n​(t):=1+t​∑m=1n(nm)​Am​(t)\tilde{A}_{n}(t):=1+t\sum_{m=1}^{n}\binom{n}{m}A_{m}(t)

as the binomial-Eulerian polynomial of degree nn. We refer to the coefficient a~n,j\tilde{a}_{n,j} of tjt^{j} in A~n​(t)\tilde{A}_{n}(t) as a binomial-Eulerian number. The binomial-Eulerian polynomials arose in the work of Postinkov, Reiner and Williams [34] as the h-polynomial of a polytope that they called the stellohedron. A qq-analog and a symmetric function analog were studied by Shareshian and Wachs [38] and further studied by González D’León [23].

Just as the Eulerian numbers enumerate permutations with a given number of descents, the binomial-Eulerian numbers enumerate partial permutations with a given number of descents, where a partial permutation of [n][n] is a permutation of a nonempty subset of [n][n]. For example, when n=3n=3, the partial permutations of [n][n] written in one line notation are:

1,2,3,12,21,13,31,23,32,123,132,213,231,312,321.1,2,3,12,21,13,31,23,32,123,132,213,231,312,321.

Let 𝔖~n\tilde{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} be the set of partial permutations of [n][n]. The descent number of a partial permutation σ=σ1σ2⋯σm\sigma=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\cdots\sigma_{m} is defined in the usual way as des(σ)=|{i∈[m−1]:σi>σi+1}|\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(\sigma)=|\{i\in[m-1]:\sigma_{i}>\sigma_{i+1}\}|. For the partial permutations listed above the respective descent numbers are:

0,0,0,0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1,1,1,2.0,0,0,0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1,1,1,1,2.

The following combinatorial characterization of A~n​(t)\tilde{A}_{n}(t) is straightforward to prove:

(3.9) A~n​(t)=1+∑σ∈𝔖~ntdes(σ)+1.\tilde{A}_{n}(t)=1+\sum_{\sigma\in\tilde{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(\sigma)+1}.

It follows from this and the list of descent numbers above that

A~3​(t)=1+7​t+7​t2+t3.\tilde{A}_{3}(t)=1+7t+7t^{2}+t^{3}.
Theorem 3.3.

For n≥1n\geq 1,

(−1)n−1​μS​tn​(t)=A~n−1​(t).(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{St_{n}}(t)=\tilde{A}_{n-1}(t).

Consequently

(−1)n−1​μS​tn​(1)=1+∑m=1n−1(n−1)m,(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{St_{n}}(1)=1+\sum_{m=1}^{n-1}(n-1)_{m},

where (n−1)m(n-1)_{m} is the falling factorial (n−1)​(n−2)​…​(n−m)(n-1)(n-2)\dots(n-m).

Proof.

The recurrence relations of Theorem 3.1 for G=S​tnG=St_{n} reduce to

∑k=0n−1(n−1k)​[k+1]t​μS​tn−k​(t)=δn,1.\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k}[k+1]_{t}\,\,\mu_{St_{n-k}}(t)=\delta_{n,1}.

This is equivalent to the exponential generating function formula

(3.10) ∑n≥0μS​tn+1​(t)​ynn!=(∑n≥0[n+1]t​ynn!)−1=t−1t​et​y−ey.\sum_{n\geq 0}\mu_{St_{n+1}}(t)\frac{y^{n}}{n!}=\left(\sum_{n\geq 0}[n+1]_{t}\frac{y^{n}}{n!}\right)^{-1}=\frac{t-1}{te^{ty}-e^{y}}.

Replacing yy by −y-y yields

∑n≥0(−1)n​μS​tn+1​(t)​ynn!\displaystyle\sum_{n\geq 0}(-1)^{n}\mu_{St_{n+1}}(t)\frac{y^{n}}{n!} =t−1t​e−t​y−e−y\displaystyle=\frac{t-1}{te^{-ty}-e^{-y}}
(3.11) =(t−1)​et​yt−e(t−1)​y.\displaystyle=\frac{(t-1)e^{ty}}{t-e^{(t-1)y}}.

It is straightforward using Euler’s exponential generating formula

(3.12) ∑n≥1An​(t)​ynn!=ey−et​yet​y−t​ey,\sum_{n\geq 1}A_{n}(t)\frac{y^{n}}{n!}=\frac{e^{y}-e^{ty}}{e^{ty}-te^{y}},

to show that the formula given in (3.11) also holds for the exponential generating function for A~n​(t)\tilde{A}_{n}(t). Indeed we have

∑n≥0A~n​(t)​ynn!\displaystyle\sum_{n\geq 0}\tilde{A}_{n}(t)\frac{y^{n}}{n!} =∑n≥0(1+t​∑m=1n(nm)​Am​(t))​ynn!\displaystyle=\sum_{n\geq 0}\left(1+t\sum_{m=1}^{n}\binom{n}{m}A_{m}(t)\right)\frac{y^{n}}{n!}
=ey+t​∑n≥1An​(t)​ynn!​∑n≥0ynn!\displaystyle=e^{y}+t\sum_{n\geq 1}A_{n}(t)\frac{y^{n}}{n!}\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{y^{n}}{n!}
=ey+t​ey−et​yet​y−t​ey​ey\displaystyle=e^{y}+t\frac{e^{y}-e^{ty}}{e^{ty}-te^{y}}e^{y}
(3.13) =(t−1)​et​yt−e(t−1)​y\displaystyle=\frac{(t-1)e^{ty}}{t-e^{(t-1)y}}

with the second to last equality following from (3.12) and the last equality following from straightforward manipulation. Comparing this with (3.11) yields the desired result. ∎

Remark 3.4.

A qq-analog and symmetric function analog of the exponential generating function formula given in (3.13) appears in [38, Propositions 4.3 and 3.3] respectively.

3.4. A connection with graph associahedra

The hh-polynomial of a simple55 5 Here we will be following the convention in [34], in which the h-polynomial is defined for simple polytopes rather than, as is often done, for simplicial polytopes. dd-dimensional polytope 𝒫\mathcal{P} is defined by

(3.14) h𝒫​(t)=∑i=0dfi​(t−1)i,\displaystyle h_{\mathcal{P}}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}f_{i}(t-1)^{i},

where fif_{i} is the number of ii dimensional faces of 𝒫\mathcal{P}.

It is well known that the Eulerian polynomials and the Narayana polynomials are hh-polynomials of simple polytopes known as the permutohedron and the associahedron, respectively. It is shown in [34] that the binomial-Eulerian polynomials are hh-polynomials of simple polytopes as well. Hence (−1)n−1​μG​(t)(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{G}(t) is, by Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 respectively, the hh-polynomial of a simple polytope when GG is the path graph PnP_{n} or the star graph S​tnSt_{n}. It is natural to ask if there are any other graphs GG for which this is the case; in this section we discuss this question.

Graph associahedra are a family of simple polytopes that were studied by Carr and Devadoss [11] and that form part of the larger class of generalized permutahedra studied by Postnikov in [35]. Several ocurrances of equivalent families have appeared in the literature as well. In particular, the dual simplicial complexes of graph associahedra are included in the family of nested set complexes studied by De Concini and Procesi in [12]. We should also mention that in recent years a great many papers have appeared with further connections between generalized permutahedra and other areas of mathematics. A paper we would like to mention is that of Aguiar and Ardila [1], in which a beautiful structure of a Hopf monoid on generalized permutahedra is described, for which the restriction to graph associahedra yields a known Hopf monoid on graphs.

We follow the notation and terminology used in [35, 34]. A building set on a finite set VV is a collection ℬ⊆2V\mathcal{B}\subseteq 2^{V} satisfying:

  • •

    {v}∈ℬ\{v\}\in\mathcal{B} for all v∈Vv\in V.

  • •

    If B,B′∈ℬB,B^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B} and B∩B′≠∅B\cap B^{\prime}\neq\emptyset then B∪B′∈ℬB\cup B^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}.

Given a graph GG on vertex set VV, one can define the building set,

ℬ⁡(G):={∅≠B⊆V∣G|B​ is connected}.\mathcal{B}(G):=\{\emptyset\neq B\subseteq V\mid G|_{B}\text{ is connected}\}.

The nestohedron 𝒫ℬ\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}} associated to a building set ℬ\mathcal{B} on V⊆[n]V\subseteq[n] is the polytope defined as the Minkowski sum

𝒫ℬ:=∑B∈ℬΔB,\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}}:=\sum_{B\in\mathcal{B}}\Delta_{B},

where the Minkowski sum of two subsets S,T∈ℝnS,T\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is defined as the subset S+T:={x+y∣x∈S​ and ​y∈T}⊆ℝnS+T:=\{x+y\mid x\in S\text{ and }y\in T\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} and ΔB\Delta_{B} is the simplex in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} obtained as the convex hull of the standard unit vectors in {𝐞i∣i∈B}\{{\bf e}_{i}\mid i\in B\}. In [35] it is shown that the nestohedron 𝒫ℬ\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}} is a simple polytope.

Nestohedra of the form 𝒫G:=𝒫ℬ⁡(G)\mathcal{P}_{G}:=\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}(G)}, where GG is a graph on V⊆[n]V\subseteq[n], are called graph-associahedra in [11]. It follows from [35, Theorem 7.11] that if G1,…,GkG_{1},\dots,G_{k} are the connected components of GG then

(3.15) h𝒫G(t)=h𝒫G1(t)⋯h𝒫Gk(t).h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t)=h_{\mathcal{P}_{G_{1}}}(t)\cdots h_{\mathcal{P}_{G_{k}}}(t).

The graph associahedron for the complete graph is the standard permutohedron and the graph associahedron for the path graph is the standard associahedron; see [34, Section 10]. The graph associahedron for the star graph is called the stellohedron in [34, Section 10.4]. As was mentioned above, it is well known that the hh-polynomials for the permutohedron and the associahedron are the Eulerian and Narayana polynomials, respectively. Thus

(3.16) h𝒫Kn​(t)\displaystyle h_{\mathcal{P}_{K_{n}}}(t) =An​(t)\displaystyle=A_{n}(t)
h𝒫Pn​(t)\displaystyle h_{\mathcal{P}_{P_{n}}}(t) =Nn​(t).\displaystyle=N_{n}(t).

In [34, Section 10.4], it is shown that,

h𝒫S​tn​(t)=A~n−1​(t).h_{\mathcal{P}_{St_{n}}}(t)=\tilde{A}_{n-1}(t).

It follows from these equations and Theorems 3.2 and 3.3 that

(−1)n−k​μG​(t)=h𝒫G​(t)(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t)=h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t)

is true for the special cases that GG is the path graph and the star graph. By (3.15) and Proposition 2.2, it is also true for forests GG whose trees are path graphs or star graphs.

In an earlier version of this paper the authors conjectured the following. For a polynomial p⁡(t)=∑i=0dai​tip(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}a_{i}t^{i}, we write p⁡(t)⪰0p(t)\succeq 0 if all its coefficients are nonnegative.

Conjecture 3.5.

For any graph GG with nn vertices and kk connected components we have that

(3.17) (−1)n−k​μG​(t)−h𝒫G​(t)⪰0,(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t)\succeq 0,

with equality if GG is a forest.

More recently, the first author together with Avila and Carrillo were able to prove this conjecture in [3, 2] and generalize it to a theorem for general building sets.

Furthermore, we observe in the following proposition that if equality in (3.17) holds then GG is necessarily a forest.

Proposition 3.6.

Let GG be a graph with nn vertices and kk connected components. If (−1)n−k​μG​(t)(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t) is equal to the hh-polynomial of a simple polytope then GG is a forest.

Proof.

The hh-polytope of every simple polytope has constant term equal to 11. Recall from Proposition 2.4 that the constant term μG​(0)\mu_{G}(0) of μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) is equal to the Möbius invariant μ⁡(ΠG)\mu(\Pi_{G}). The result now follows from the known fact that (−1)n−k​μ​(ΠG)=1(-1)^{n-k}\mu(\Pi_{G})=1 if and only if GG is a forest. One can prove this by using Whitney’s Broken Circuit Theorem [47], which tells us that (−1)n−k​μ​(ΠG)(-1)^{n-k}\mu(\Pi_{G}) is equal to the number of spanning forests of GG that contain no broken circuits. (A broken circuit is a subgraph of GG obtained by removing the smallest edge, under a fixed total ordering of the edges of GG, from a cycle of GG.) ∎

By Theorem 3.1, the following recurrence relations are consequences of Conjecture 3.5 (now proved in [3, 2] as noted above).

Corollary 3.7.

Let TT be a tree on node set [n][n]. If n>1n>1 then

(3.18) h𝒫T​(t)=∑π∈ΠT∖{1^}(−1)|π|​[|π|]t​∏B∈πh𝒫T|B​(t)h_{\mathcal{P}_{T}}(t)=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{T}\setminus\{\hat{1}\}}(-1)^{|\pi|}[|\pi|]_{t}\prod_{B\in\pi}h_{\mathcal{P}_{T|_{B}}}(t)

and

(3.19) h𝒫T​(t)=∑π∈ΠT∖{0^}(−1)n−|π|−1​h𝒫T/π​(t)​∏B∈π[|B|]t.h_{\mathcal{P}_{T}}(t)=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{T}\setminus\{\hat{0}\}}(-1)^{n-|\pi|-1}h_{\mathcal{P}_{T/\pi}}(t)\prod_{B\in\pi}[|B|]_{t}.
Remark 3.8.

In [35, Theorem 7.11], Postnikov gives a recurrence for h𝒫ℬ​(t)h_{\mathcal{P}_{\mathcal{B}}}(t), where ℬ\mathcal{B} is a building set. If one applies this to ℬ⁡(T)\mathcal{B}(T), where TT is a tree, one gets a recurrence relation that is different from those in the conjectured Corollary  3.7. Indeed the recurrence relation in [35] for trees TT is

h𝒫T​(t)=∑U⊊[n](t−1)n−|U|−1​∏R∈T|Uh𝒫R​(t),h_{\mathcal{P}_{T}}(t)=\sum_{U\subsetneq[n]}(t-1)^{n-|U|-1}\prod_{R\in T|_{U}}h_{\mathcal{P}_{R}}(t),

where the forest T|UT|_{U} is viewed as a set of trees.

4. γ\gamma-positivity for chordal graphs

In this section we discuss a property of polynomials in ℝ⁡[t]\mathbb{R}[t] called γ\gamma-positivity. Postnikov, Reiner, and Williams [34] established this property for hh-polynomials of graph associahedra of chordal graphs and here we do the same for Möbius polynomials. We review their γ\gamma-positivity result in Section 4.1 for the sake of comparison with our analogous result presented in Section 4.2.

Let p⁡(t)=∑j=0daj​tj∈ℝ⁡[t]p(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_{j}t^{j}\in\mathbb{R}[t]. Recall that p⁡(t)p(t) is said to be palindromic if aj=ad−ja_{j}=a_{d-j} for all jj, and p⁡(t)p(t) is said to be unimodal if

(4.1) 0≤a0≤a1≤⋯≤ac≥⋯≥ad−1≥ad≥0,0\leq a_{0}\leq a_{1}\leq\cdots\leq a_{c}\geq\cdots\geq a_{d-1}\geq a_{d}\geq 0,

for some c∈{0,1,…,d}c\in\{0,1,\dots,d\}. Note that if p⁡(t)p(t) is palindromic and unimodal and a0>0a_{0}>0 (which means dd is the degree of p⁡(t)p(t)) then all the coefficients of p⁡(t)p(t) are positive, denoted p⁡(t)≻0p(t)\succ 0.

It is straightforward to see that p⁡(t)p(t) is palindromic if and only if

p⁡(t)=∑j=0⌊d2⌋γj​tj​(1+t)d−2​jp(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor\frac{d}{2}\rfloor}\gamma_{j}t^{j}(1+t)^{d-2j}

for some γj∈ℝ\gamma_{j}\in\mathbb{R}. The coefficients γj\gamma_{j} are commonly called γ\gamma-coefficients. If γj≥0\gamma_{j}\geq 0 for all jj then the polynomial p⁡(t)p(t) is said to be γ\gamma-positive.66 6 This is often called γ\gamma-nonnegative. It is well known and straightforward to prove that if p⁡(t)p(t) is γ\gamma-positive then p⁡(t)p(t) is both palindromic and unimodal.

A celebrated result of Stanley [40] asserts that the hh-polynomial of any convex simple polytope is unimodal as well as palindromic (which was already well-known). Interest in γ\gamma-positivity stems in part from Gal’s conjecture [17] which in the case of convex polytopes asserts that the hh-polynomial of any simple flag polytope is γ\gamma-positive.

A graph is said to be chordal if it does not have any induced cycles of length greater than 33. Chordal graphs are exactly those that admit a (reverse) perfect elimination order (PEO), i.e., a total order of the vertices v1,v2,…,vnv_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{n} such that for every ii the set of neighbors vjv_{j} of viv_{i}, such that j<ij<i, form a clique, see [34, Section 9.2].

We will say that a graph GG on vertex set V={v1,v2,…,vn}⊂ℤ>0V=\{v_{1},v_{2},\dots,v_{n}\}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{>0} is a perfectly labeled chordal graph if the natural order v1<v2<⋯<vnv_{1}<v_{2}<\dots<v_{n} is a PEO for GG. Note that every chordal graph is isomorphic to a perfectly labeled chordal graph. The complete graph on [n][n] is a perfectly labeled chordal graph, as is every increasing tree on [n][n], where a tree on [n][n] is increasing if when rooted at 11, every vertex is smaller than its children.

4.1. hh-polynomials of chordal graph associahedra

In [34], Postnikov, Reiner, and Williams establish γ\gamma-positivity of the hh-polynomial of the graph associahedron of any chordal graph, thereby confirming Gal’s conjecture for this class of flag simple polytopes.77 7 They do this more generally for chordal nestohedron. They do this by giving a combinatorial characterization of the coefficients and the γ\gamma-coefficients of the hh-polynomial in terms of a certain set of permutations. We review this result in this section.

For any graph GG on vertex set [n][n], a GG-permutation88 8 Note that max\max is used instead of min\min in [34]. Hence, the roles of descents and ascents are exchanged. is a permutation σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} such that for every i∈[n]i\in[n], the elements σ⁡(i)\sigma(i) and min⁡{σ⁡(1),…,σ⁡(i)}\min\{\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(i)\} are in the same connected component of G|{σ⁡(1),…,σ⁡(i)}G|_{\{\sigma(1),\dots,\sigma(i)\}}. Let 𝔖⁡(G)\mathfrak{S}(G) be the set of GG-permutations and let 𝔖^​(G):=𝔖⁡(G)∩𝔖^n\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}(G):=\mathfrak{S}(G)\cap\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}, where 𝔖^n\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} is the subset of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} consisting of permutations σ\sigma with no consecutive ascents; that is for all i∈[n−2]i\in[n-2], if σ⁡(i)<σ⁡(i+1)\sigma(i)<\sigma(i+1) then σ⁡(i+1)>σ⁡(i+2)\sigma(i+1)>\sigma(i+2).99 9 Note that in [34], 𝔖^n\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} denotes a smaller subset in which a final descent is also required. For σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}, let

asc(σ)=|{i∈[n−1]:σ⁡(i)<σ⁡(i+1)}|.\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)=|\{i\in[n-1]:\sigma(i)<\sigma(i+1)\}|.
Theorem 4.1 (Postnikov, Reiner, Williams [34]).

For n≥1n\geq 1 and GG a connected perfectly labeled chordal graph on [n][n], we have that

(4.2) h𝒫G​(t)=∑σ∈𝔖⁡(G)tasc(σ)h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t)=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}(G)}t^{\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)}

and

(4.3) h𝒫G​(t)=∑σ∈𝔖^​(G)σ⁡(n−1)>σ⁡(n)tasc(σ)​(1+t)n−1−2​asc(σ).h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}(G)\\ \sigma(n-1)>\sigma(n)\end{subarray}}t^{\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)}(1+t)^{n-1-2\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)}.

Now by (3.15) and the fact that products of γ\gamma-positive polynomials are γ\gamma-positive we have the following consequence.

Corollary 4.2.

If GG is a chordal graph then h𝒫G​(t)h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t) is γ\gamma-positive.

Example 4.3.

(1) For G=KnG=K_{n}, we have 𝔖⁡(G)=𝔖n\mathfrak{S}(G)=\mathfrak{S}_{n}. Thus, in this case, (4.2) reduces to the combinatorial definition of the Eulerian polynomial given in (3.8), and (4.3) reduces to a well known formula of Foata and Schützenberger [16, Theorem 5.6] for the Eulerian polynomials.

σ⁡(1)>σ⁡(2)>⋯>σ⁡(k)=1\sigma(1)>\sigma(2)>\dots>\sigma(k)=1

for some k∈[n+1]k\in[n+1]. Thus, in this case, (4.2) reduces to a formula equivalent to the combinatorial characterization of the binomial-Eulerian polynomials given in (3.9), and (4.3) reduces to the formula

(4.4) A~n​(t)=∑σ∈𝔖^n+1σ⁡(n)>σ⁡(n+1)σ⁡(1)>σ⁡(2)>⋯>σ⁡(k)=1tasc(σ)​(1+t)n−1−2​asc(σ).\tilde{A}_{n}(t)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n+1}\\ \sigma(n)>\sigma(n+1)\\ \sigma(1)>\sigma(2)>\dots>\sigma(k)=1\end{subarray}}t^{\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)}(1+t)^{n-1-2\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)}.

4.2. Möbius polynomials of chordal graphs

In this subsection we present results for Möbius polynomials that are analogous to the results for hh-polynomials reviewed in Section 4.1.

By binary tree we mean a planar rooted tree in which every internal node has a left child and a right child. A leaf-labeled binary tree is a binary tree whose leaves are labeled with distinct labels. If AA is the set of leaf labels of the binary tree TT we say that TT is a binary tree on leaf set AA. Let ℬ​𝒯n\mathcal{BT}_{n} denote the set of binary trees on leaf set [n][n].

For each node xx of T∈ℬ​𝒯nT\in\mathcal{BT}_{n}, let

  • •

    AxA_{x} be the subset of [n][n] consisting of the leaf labels of the subtree rooted at xx

  • •

    L⁡(x)L(x) be the left child of xx

  • •

    R⁡(x)R(x) be the right child of xx.

We say that T∈ℬ​𝒯nT\in\mathcal{BT}_{n} is normalized if

min⁡AL⁡(x)<min⁡AR⁡(x)\min A_{L(x)}<\min A_{R(x)}

for all internal nodes xx of TT. Let

𝒩n={T∈ℬ​𝒯n:T​ is normalized}.\mathcal{N}_{n}=\{T\in\mathcal{BT}_{n}:T\mbox{ is normalized}\}.

We say that an internal node xx of T∈𝒩nT\in\mathcal{N}_{n} is a Lyndon node if its left child is a leaf or

(4.5) min⁡AR⁡(L⁡(x))>min⁡AR⁡(x).\min A_{R(L(x))}>\min A_{R(x)}.

We refer to these nodes as Lyndon nodes because the classical Lyndon trees are the normalized binary trees in which all internal nodes are Lyndon. Now let

𝒩n^={T∈𝒩n:∀x∈𝐢𝐧𝐭(T), x is not Lyndon ⟹L⁡(x) is Lyndon},\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{n}}=\{T\in\mathcal{N}_{n}:\forall x\in{\bf\mathop{int}}(T),\mbox{ $x$ is not Lyndon $\implies L(x)$ is Lyndon}\},

where 𝐢𝐧𝐭(T){\bf\mathop{int}}(T) is the set of internal nodes of TT. See Figure 4.1 for an example of a tree in 𝒩n^\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{n}} and a normalized tree not in 𝒩n^\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{n}}.

Let GG be a graph on vertex set [n][n]. Define

𝒩G:={T∈𝒩n:G|Ax​ is connected ​∀x∈𝐢𝐧𝐭(T)}\mathcal{N}_{G}:=\{T\in\mathcal{N}_{n}:G|_{A_{x}}\mbox{ is connected }\forall x\in{\bf\mathop{int}}(T)\}

and

𝒩G^:=𝒩G∩𝒩n^.\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{G}}:=\mathcal{N}_{G}\cap\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{n}}.

The proof of the following theorem is deferred to Section 6.3, where the more general Theorem 6.18 is proved.

Theorem 4.4.

Let GG be a connected perfectly labeled chordal graph on vertex set [n][n]. Then

(−1)n−1​μG​(t)=∑T∈𝒩G^tm⁡(T)​(1+t)n−1−2​m​(T),(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{G}(t)=\sum_{T\in\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{G}}}t^{m(T)}(1+t)^{n-1-2m(T)},

where m⁡(T)m(T) is the number of nonLyndon internal nodes of TT.

Let GG be P4P_{4} with the additional edge {1,3}\{1,3\}. Since GG is a perfectly labeled chordal graph, we can apply Theorem 4.4. In Figure 4.2, the trees of 𝒩G^\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{G}} are listed and their nonLyndon nodes are indicated. By Theorem 4.4, we have that

−μG​(t)=2​(1+t)3+5​t​(1+t).-\mu_{G}(t)=2(1+t)^{3}+5t(1+t).

Corollary 4.6.

Let GG be a chordal graph with nn vertices and kk connected components. Then (−1)n−k​μG​(t)(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t) is γ\gamma-positive.

Proof.

This follows from Theorem 4.4, Proposition 2.2, and the fact that products of γ\gamma-positive polynomials are γ\gamma-positive. ∎

Corollary 4.7.

Let GG and HH be perfectly labeled chordal graphs with nn vertices and kk connected components. If HH is a subgraph of GG then (−1)n−k​(μG​(t)−μH​(t))(-1)^{n-k}(\mu_{G}({t})-\mu_{H}({t})) is γ\gamma-positive.

Proof.

In the connected case, this result follows immediately from Theorem 4.4, since clearly 𝒩H^⊆𝒩G^\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{H}}\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{G}}. In the general case we also use Proposition 2.2. Details are given in the proof of the more general Corollary 6.20. ∎

Corollary 4.8.

Let GG and HH be perfectly labeled chordal graphs with nn vertices and kk connected components. Then

(4.6) (−1)n−k​μG​(t)≻0.(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t)\succ 0.

If HH is a subgraph of GG then

(4.7) (−1)n−k​(μG​(t)−μH​(t))≻0.(-1)^{n-k}(\mu_{G}({t})-\mu_{H}({t}))\succ 0.
Proof.

Equation (4.6) follows from Corollary 4.6 and the the fact that μG​(0)≠0\mu_{G}(0)\neq 0, cf. Proposition 2.4.

Equation (4.7) follows from Corollary 4.7 and the the fact that μG​(0)−μH​(0)≠0\mu_{G}(0)-\mu_{H}(0)\neq 0. Through a similar argument to the one used in proof of Proposition 3.6, one can prove this fact by using Whitney’s Broken Circuit Theorem [47]. Indeed, removing one edge that does not increase the number of connected components decreases the number of spanning forests that are free of broken circuits. ∎

Let GG be the graph in Example 4.5 and let H=P4H=P_{4}. We have

−(μG​(t)−μH​(t))\displaystyle-(\mu_{G}(t)-\mu_{H}(t)) =2​(1+t)3+5​t​(1+t)−((1+t)3+3​t​(1+t))\displaystyle=2(1+t)^{3}+5t(1+t)-((1+t)^{3}+3t(1+t))
=(1+t)3+2​t​(1+t),\displaystyle=(1+t)^{3}+2t(1+t),

Example 4.10.

We apply Theorem 4.4 to the path graphs. A binary tree TT on leaf set [n][n] is in 𝒩Pn\mathcal{N}_{P_{n}} if and only if the leaves of TT are labeled from left to right in increasing order. Consequently, the only Lyndon nodes of TT are the internal nodes whose left child is a leaf. Since there can be only one leaf labeling for the trees in 𝒩Pn\mathcal{N}_{P_{n}}, we can view these trees as unlabeled binary trees. Thus by Theorems 3.2 and 4.4, we get the following combinatorial interpretation of the Narayana polynomials

Nn​(t)=∑Ttm⁡(T)​(1+t)n−1−2​m​(T),N_{n}(t)=\sum_{T}t^{m(T)}(1+t)^{n-1-2m(T)},

where the sum is taken over the unlabeled binary trees TT with nn leaves in which the left child of every left child is a leaf, and m⁡(T)m(T) is the number of internal nodes of TT that are left children.

Let σT\sigma_{T} be the permutation in 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} defined by letting σT​(i)=σ⁡(i+1)−1\sigma_{T}(i)=\sigma(i+1)-1 for all i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1]. It follows that T∈𝒩S​tn+1^T\in\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{St_{n+1}}} if and only if σT\sigma_{T} has no consecutive ascents. Thus by Theorems 3.3 and 4.4,

(4.8) A~n​(t)=∑σ∈𝔖^ntasc(σ)​(1+t)n−2​asc(σ),\tilde{A}_{n}(t)=\sum_{\sigma\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}}t^{\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)}(1+t)^{n-2\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)},

where 𝔖^n\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n} is the set of permutations in 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} with no consecutive ascents and asc(σ)\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma) is the number of ascents of σ\sigma. This combinatorial description of the γ\gamma-coefficients of A~n​(t)\tilde{A}_{n}(t) was previously obtained in [38], along with a qq-analog and a symmetric function analog.

Note that the Postnikov-Reiner-Williams formula (4.4) yields a different combinatorial description of the γ\gamma-coefficients. Equating the two descriptions yields

|{σ∈𝔖^n|asc(σ)=j}|=|\{\sigma\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}|\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)=j\}|=
|{σ∈𝔖^n+1|σ(n)>σ(n+1),σ(i)>σ(i+1)∀i∈[σ−1(1)−1],asc(σ)=j}|.|\{\sigma\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n+1}|\sigma(n)>\sigma(n+1),\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)\forall i\in[\sigma^{-1}(1)-1],\mathop{\rm asc}\nolimits(\sigma)=j\}|.

A nice bijective proof of this was obtained by Ellzey [15].

We observe that (4.6) (without the chordality assumption) is a consequence of Conjecture 3.5, which as was noted above was proved in [3, 2]. Indeed this follows from the fact that the hh-polynomial of any convex simple polytope has positive coefficients. We think it likely that other results discussed above also hold without the chordality assumption. Item (1) of the following conjecture has been tested by computer for connected graphs with up to 77 vertices.

Conjecture 4.12.

Let GG be a graph with nn vertices and kk connected components. Then

  1. (1)

    (−1)n−k​μG​(t)(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t) is γ\gamma-positive.

  2. (2)

    If HH is a subgraph of GG with nn vertices and kk connected components then

    (−1)n−k​(μG​(t)−μH​(t))(-1)^{n-k}(\mu_{G}({t})-\mu_{H}({t}))

    is γ\gamma-positive.

It is well known that all real-rooted palindromic polynomials with nonnegative real coefficients are γ\gamma-positive; see [10]. Since by Proposition 2.4, μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) is palindromic for all GG, we conjecture the following.

Conjecture 4.13.

Let GG be a graph with nn vertices and kk connected components. Then

  1. (1)

    (−1)n−k​μG​(t)(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t) is real-rooted.

  2. (2)

    If HH is a subgraph of GG with nn vertices and kk connected components then

    (−1)n−k​(μG​(t)−μH​(t))(-1)^{n-k}(\mu_{G}({t})-\mu_{H}({t}))

    is real-rooted.

We have verified (1) by computer for all connected graphs with up to 77 vertices. It follows from (3.4) that (1) holds for the complete graph. It is known that the Narayana polynomials are real-rooted (see [33, Exercise 4.7]) and more recently, Haglund and Zang [27] established real-rootedness, for the binomial-Eulerian polynomials. Avila, Carrillo, and the first author prove (1) in the case of the cycle graph in [3, 2]. Hence by Theorems 3.2 and 3.3, and Proposition 2.2, item (1) is valid for all graphs whose connected components are complete graphs, path graphs, star graphs, or cycle graphs.

Next we consider the polynomial (−1)n−k​μG​(t)−h𝒫G​(t)(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t) of Conjecture 3.5. (As noted above this conjecture has now been proved in [3, 2].) Palindromicity of this polynomial follows from the fact that μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) and h𝒫G​(t)h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t) are both palindromic with the same center of symmetry. Note that this polynomial fails to be γ\gamma-positive already for G=K3G=K_{3}. Indeed, μK3​(t)−h𝒫K3​(t)=1+t+t2\mu_{K_{3}}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{K_{3}}}(t)=1+t+t^{2}. However, note that the weaker unimodality property still holds for K3K_{3}. In fact, as we see in the next result, it holds for all complete graphs.

Theorem 4.14.

For all n≥1n\geq 1, the polynomial (−1)n−1​μKn​(t)−h𝒫Kn​(t)(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{K_{n}}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{K_{n}}}(t) is palindromic and unimodal. Moreover, (−1)n−1​μKn​(t)−h𝒫Kn​(t)≻0(-1)^{n-1}\mu_{K_{n}}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{K_{n}}}(t)\succ 0.

Proof.

By (3.5), (3.8) and (3.16), we have

(−1)n−k​μKn​(t)−h𝒫Kn​(t)=∑T∈𝒰​𝒯n∑w∈L⁡(T)tdes(T,w)−∑σ∈𝔖ntdes(σ),(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{K_{n}}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{K_{n}}}(t)=\sum_{T\in\mathcal{UT}_{n}}\,\sum_{w\in L(T)}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(T,w)}-\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(\sigma)},

where 𝒰​𝒯n\mathcal{UT}_{n} is the set of unlabeled nonplanar rooted trees with nn nodes and L⁡(T)L(T) is the set of labelings of TT. Since permutations can be viewed as labeled linear nonplanar rooted trees, we have that

(−1)n−k​μKn​(t)−h𝒫Kn​(t)=∑T∈𝒰​𝒯¯n∑w∈L⁡(T)tdes(T,w),(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{K_{n}}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{K_{n}}}(t)=\sum_{T\in\overline{\mathcal{UT}}_{n}}\,\sum_{w\in L(T)}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(T,w)},

where 𝒰​𝒯¯n\overline{\mathcal{UT}}_{n} is the set of nonlinear unlabeled nonplanar rooted trees with nn nodes. Now for each T∈𝒰​𝒯nT\in{\mathcal{UT}}_{n}, we claim that ∑w∈L⁡(T)tdes(T,w)\sum_{w\in L(T)}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(T,w)} is palindromic and unimodal. Indeed, this follows from [25, Lemma 2.2 and Theorem 2.3], which gives the claimed result for rooted planar trees. Since the polynomial ∑w∈L⁡(T)tdes(T,w)\sum_{w\in L(T)}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(T,w)} when TT is planar is a constant multiple of the polynomial when TT is nonplanar, we can conclude that our claim holds. Since every tree has both an increasing and a decreasing labeling, the polynomial ∑w∈L⁡(T)tdes(T,w)\sum_{w\in L(T)}t^{\mathop{\rm des}\nolimits(T,w)} has strictly positive constant term and degree n−1n-1 for all T∈𝒰​𝒯nT\in{\mathcal{UT}}_{n}. The result now follows from the fact that the sum of palindromic unimodal polynomials with the same center of symmetry is palindromic and unimodal. ∎

The result for KnK_{n} leads us to make the following conjecture, which is stronger than Conjecture 3.5 and is still open. We have checked this by computer for all graphs with up to n=7n=7 vertices.

Conjecture 4.15.

For any graph GG with nn vertices and kk connected components, the palindromic polynomial (−1)n−k​μG​(t)−h𝒫G​(t)(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t) is unimodal, and all its coefficients are positive.

The following even stronger conjecture has also been checked by computer for all graphs with up to n=7n=7 vertices.

Conjecture 4.16.

For a graph GG with nn vertices and kk connected components, the palindromic polynomial (−1)n−k​μG​(t)−h𝒫G​(t)(-1)^{n-k}\mu_{G}(t)-h_{\mathcal{P}_{G}}(t) is log-concave, in the sense of (7.5), and all its coefficients are positive.

5. Multiweighted bond posets and Möbius symmetric functions

In [22] González D’León considers a generalization of the weighted partition poset based on the observation that a weighted block BuB^{u} of a weighted partition can be written as B(u,|B|−1−u)B^{(u,|B|-1-u)} thereby using weights that are pairs of nonnegative integers rather than single nonnegative integers. To merge two bi-weighted blocks, B1(μ⁡(1),μ⁡(2))B_{1}^{(\mu(1),\mu(2))} and B2(ν⁡(1),ν⁡(2))B_{2}^{(\nu(1),\nu(2))}, now means to form either the bi-weighted block (B1∪B2)(μ⁡(1)+ν⁡(1)+1,μ⁡(2)+ν⁡(2))(B_{1}\cup B_{2})^{(\mu(1)+\nu(1)+1,\mu(2)+\nu(2))} or the biweighted block (B1∪B2)(μ⁡(1)+ν⁡(1),μ⁡(2)+ν⁡(2)+1)(B_{1}\cup B_{2})^{(\mu(1)+\nu(1),\mu(2)+\nu(2)+1)}. By using weights that are rr-tuples instead of pairs, one gets the more general rr-weighted partition poset studied in [22]. In this section we generalize the notion of weighted bond posets to rr-weighted bond posets. This leads to a symmetric function generalization of the Möbius polynomial μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) and symmetric function generalizations of the results for μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t) discussed in earlier sections.

5.1. Preliminaries

For r>0r>0, a weak rr-composition of an integer m≥0m\geq 0 is an rr-tuple ν=(ν⁡(1),μ⁡(2),…,ν⁡(r))\nu=(\nu(1),\mu(2),\dots,\nu(r)) of nonnegative integers whose sum ∑i=1rν⁡(i)\sum_{i=1}^{r}\nu(i) equals mm. We denote by WCompm,r{\rm WComp}_{m,r} the set of weak rr-compositions of mm. For μ=(μ⁡(1),…,μ⁡(r))∈WCompm,r\mu=(\mu(1),\dots,\mu(r))\in{\rm WComp}_{m,r} and ν=(ν⁡(1),…,ν⁡(r))∈WCompn,r\nu=(\nu(1),\dots,\nu(r))\in{\rm WComp}_{n,r}, let

μ+ν:=(μ⁡(1)+ν⁡(1),…,μ⁡(r)+ν⁡(r))∈WCompm+n,r.\mu+\nu:=(\mu(1)+\nu(1),\dots,\mu(r)+\nu(r))\in{\rm WComp}_{m+n,r}.

We say μ≥ν\mu\geq\nu if

μ−ν:=(μ⁡(1)−ν⁡(1),…,μ⁡(r)−ν⁡(r))∈WCompm−n,r.\mu-\nu:=(\mu(1)-\nu(1),\dots,\mu(r)-\nu(r))\in{\rm WComp}_{m-n,r}.

Let 𝟎\bf 0 denote the rr-tuple of 00’s and for each i=1,…,ri=1,\dots,r, let 𝐞𝐢{\bf e_{i}} denote the rr-tuple with a 11 in the iith component and 00’s elsewhere.

By padding with 00’s we can view weak rr-compositions of mm as ss-compositions of mm for s>rs>r. Thus we can say

WCompm,1⊂WCompm,2⊂WCompm,3⊂⋯,{\rm WComp}_{m,1}\subset{\rm WComp}_{m,2}\subset{\rm WComp}_{m,3}\subset\cdots,

and define

WCompm:=WCompm,∞:=⋃r≥1WCompm,r.{\rm WComp}_{m}:={\rm WComp}_{m,\infty}:=\bigcup_{r\geq 1}{\rm WComp}_{m,r}.

We can view WCompm{\rm WComp}_{m} as the set of infinite sequences of nonnegative integers whose sum is mm. We call these infinite sequences weak ∞\infty-compositions of mm or just weak compositions of mm.

For r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}, an rr-weighted partition of a set SS is defined to be a set of the form 𝝅={B1ν1,B2ν2,…,Bkνk}\boldsymbol{\pi}=\{B_{1}^{\nu_{1}},B_{2}^{\nu_{2}},...,B_{k}^{\nu_{k}}\}, where {B1,B2,…,Bk}\{B_{1},B_{2},...,B_{k}\} is a partition of SS and νi∈WComp|Bi|−1,r\nu_{i}\in{\rm WComp}_{|B_{i}|-1,r} for all i∈[k]i\in[k]. In what follows, it will be convenient to let [∞][\infty] denote ℤ>0\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.

The poset of rr-weighted partitions ΠSr\Pi_{S}^{r} is the set of rr-weighted partitions of SS with order relation defined by

{A1μ1,A2μ2,…,Ajμj}≤{B1ν1,B2ν2,…,Bkνk}\{A_{1}^{\mu_{1}},A_{2}^{\mu_{2}},...,A_{j}^{\mu_{j}}\}\leq\{B_{1}^{\nu_{1}},B_{2}^{\nu_{2}},...,B_{k}^{\nu_{k}}\}

if the following conditions hold:

  • •

    {A1,A2,…,Aj}≤{B1,B2,…,Bk}\{A_{1},A_{2},...,A_{j}\}\leq\{B_{1},B_{2},...,B_{k}\} in ΠS\Pi_{S}

  • •

    if Bm=Ai1∪Ai2∪…∪AilB_{m}=A_{i_{1}}\cup A_{i_{2}}\cup...\cup A_{i_{l}} then

    νm≥μi1+μi2+…+μil.\nu_{m}\geq\mu_{i_{1}}+\mu_{i_{2}}+...+\mu_{i_{l}}.

The covering relation ⋖\lessdot is given by

{A1μ1,A2μ2,…,Ajμj}⋖{B1ν1,B2ν2,…,Bkνk}\{A_{1}^{\mu_{1}},A_{2}^{\mu_{2}},...,A_{j}^{\mu_{j}}\}\lessdot\{B_{1}^{\nu_{1}},B_{2}^{\nu_{2}},...,B_{k}^{\nu_{k}}\}

if and only if the following conditions hold:

  • •

    {A1,A2,…,Aj}⋖{B1,B2,…,Bk}\{A_{1},A_{2},\dots,A_{j}\}\lessdot\{B_{1},B_{2},\dots,B_{k}\} in ΠS\Pi_{S}

  • •

    if Bm=Ah∪AiB_{m}=A_{h}\cup A_{i}, where h≠ih\neq i, then νm−(μh+μi)=𝐞𝐬\nu_{m}-(\mu_{h}+\mu_{i})=\mathbf{e_{s}} for some s∈[r]s\in[r].

  • •

    if Bm=AiB_{m}=A_{i} then νm=μi\nu_{m}=\mu_{i}.

Note that when r=1r=1, the rr-weighted partition poset ΠSr\Pi_{S}^{r} is isomorphic to ΠS\Pi_{S} and when r=2r=2, the rr-weighted partition poset ΠSr\Pi_{S}^{r} is isomorphic to the weighted partition poset 𝒲​ΠS\mathcal{W}\Pi_{S}. Indeed, the map taking the biweighted partition B1ν1​|⋯|​BkνkB_{1}^{\nu_{1}}|\cdots|B_{k}^{\nu_{k}} to the single weighted partition B1ν1​(1)​|⋯|​Bkνk​(1)B_{1}^{\nu_{1}(1)}|\cdots|B_{k}^{\nu_{k}(1)} is an isomorphism from ΠS2\Pi_{S}^{2} to 𝒲​ΠS\mathcal{W}\Pi_{S}.

Let Πnr:=Π[n]r\Pi^{r}_{n}:=\Pi_{[n]}^{r}. See Figure 5.1 for the Hasse diagram of Π33\Pi_{3}^{3}.

Remark 5.1.

In [22] González D’León obtains results connecting the rr-weighted partition poset Πnr\Pi_{n}^{r} to the free Lie algebra with rr compatible brackets. These results generalize classical results in the r=1r=1 case, and results of both authors [20] in the r=2r=2 case.

Given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}, we define the rr-weighted bond poset ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r} of GG to be the induced subposet of ΠVr\Pi_{V}^{r} consisting of rr-weighted partitions {B1ν1,…,Bkνk}\{B_{1}^{\nu_{1}},\dots,B_{k}^{\nu_{k}}\} whose underlying partition {B1,…,Bk}\{B_{1},\dots,B_{k}\} is in ΠG\Pi_{G}, that is, for each ii, the induced subgraph G|BiG|_{B_{i}} is connected. Note that ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r} is finite if and only if rr is finite or E=∅E=\emptyset.

Clearly, for all rr,

ΠKnr=Πnr.\Pi_{K_{n}}^{r}=\Pi_{n}^{r}.

Note that for all graphs GG,

ΠG1≃ΠG​ and ​ΠG2≃𝒲​ΠG.\Pi_{G}^{1}\simeq\Pi_{G}\,\,\mbox{ and }\,\,\Pi_{G}^{2}\simeq\mathcal{W}\Pi_{G}.

See Figure 5.2 for the Hasse diagram of ΠP33\Pi_{P_{3}}^{3}.

Just as for the r=2r=2 case discused in Section 2, for 𝜶≤𝜷\boldsymbol{\alpha}\leq\boldsymbol{\beta} in ΠGr\Pi^{r}_{G}, let [𝜶,𝜷]G[\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}]_{G} denote the closed interval {𝝅∈ΠGr:𝜶≤𝝅≤𝜷}\{\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\Pi_{G}^{r}:\boldsymbol{\alpha}\leq\boldsymbol{\pi}\leq\boldsymbol{\beta}\}. When G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is connected, again we drop the set brackets for the maximal elements {Vν}\{V^{\nu}\} of ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r}.

For each graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with kk connected components, and r∈ℤ≥1∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\cup\{\infty\}, the poset ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r} is pure of length |V|−k|V|-k. It has minimum element 0^:=v1𝟎​|⋯|​vn𝟎\hat{0}:=v_{1}^{\mathbf{0}}|\cdots|v_{n}^{\mathbf{0}}, where V={v1,…,vn}V=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{n}\}, and if GG is connected, ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r} has maximal element {Vν}\{V^{\nu}\} (which we write as VνV^{\nu}) for each ν∈WCompn−1,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r}.

Proposition 2.1 generalizes to rr-weighted bond posets ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r}.

Proposition 5.2.

Let GG be a graph whose connected components are G1,…,GkG_{1},\dots,G_{k}. Then for all r∈ℤ≥1∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}\cup\{\infty\}, the map

φ:ΠrG1×⋯×ΠrGk→ΠrG\varphi:\Pi^{r}_{G_{1}}\times\cdots\times\Pi^{r}_{G_{k}}\to\Pi^{r}_{G}

defined by φ⁡(𝛑1,…,𝛑k)=𝛑1∪⋯∪𝛑k\varphi(\boldsymbol{\pi}_{1},\dots,\boldsymbol{\pi}_{k})=\boldsymbol{\pi}_{1}\cup\cdots\cup\boldsymbol{\pi}_{k} is a poset isomorphism.

The following result is straightforward to prove.

Proposition 5.3.

Let GG be a graph on vertex set VV and let r,s∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}.

  1. (1)

    If r<sr<s then each maximal interval of ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r} is isomorphic to a maximal interval of ΠGs\Pi_{G}^{s}

  2. (2)

    Suppose α∈WCompn−1,r\alpha\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r} and β∈WCompn−1,s\beta\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,s} have the same multiset of nonzero entries. If GG is connected then the maximal intervals [0^,Vα]G[\hat{0},V^{\alpha}]_{G} and [0^,Vβ]G[\hat{0},V^{\beta}]_{G} are isomorphic.

5.2. Möbius symmetric functions

We are now ready to define the graph invariant that generalizes the Möbius polynomial defined in Section 2.

For any graph GG, the Möbius symmetric function of GG in infinitely many variables 𝐱=(x1,x2,…)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},x_{2},\dots) is defined by

MG​(𝐱):=∑𝝅∈Max(ΠG∞)μΠG∞​(0^,𝝅)​𝐱w⁡(𝝅),M_{G}(\mathbf{x}):=\sum_{\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\mathop{\rm Max}\nolimits(\Pi_{G}^{\infty})}\mu_{\Pi_{G}^{\infty}}(\hat{0},\boldsymbol{\pi})\mathbf{x}^{w(\boldsymbol{\pi})},

where, 𝐱ν=x1ν⁡(1)x2ν⁡(2)⋯\mathbf{x}^{\nu}=x_{1}^{\nu(1)}x_{2}^{\nu(2)}\cdots for ν∈WCompm,∞\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{m,\infty}, and w⁡(𝝅)w(\boldsymbol{\pi}) is the sum of the weights of the blocks of 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi}. (Recall Max(P)\mathop{\rm Max}\nolimits(P) is the set of maximal elements of a poset PP.) It follows from Proposition 5.3 that MG​(𝐱)M_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is indeed a symmetric function. Moreover, if GG has nn vertices and kk connected components then MG​(𝐱)M_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is a homogeneous symmetric function of degree n−kn-k. This is in fact the highest degree homogeneous component of the symmetric function defined in Equation (7.1) which, as we observe in Section 7, is a symmetric function analog of the chromatic polynomial of GG.

Note that if GG is a connected graph on vertex set VV then

MG​(𝐱)=∑ν∈WComp|V|−1μΠG∞​(0^,Vν)​𝐱ν.M_{G}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{|V|-1}}\mu_{\Pi_{G}^{\infty}}(\hat{0},V^{\nu})\mathbf{x}^{\nu}.

Moreover, it follows from Proposition 5.3 that by viewing partitions of mm as weak compositions of mm (by padding with zeros), we have for connected GG,

MG​(𝐱)=∑λ⊢|V|−1μΠG∞​(0^,Vλ)​mλ​(𝐱),M_{G}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\lambda\vdash|V|-1}\mu_{\Pi_{G}^{\infty}}(\hat{0},V^{\lambda})m_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}),

where mλm_{\lambda} is the monomial symmetric function indexed by the partition λ\lambda.

It also follows from Proposition 5.3 that for all rr,

MG(x1,…,xr,0,0,…)=∑𝝅∈Max(ΠGr)μΠGr(0^,𝝅)x1w​(𝝅)​(1)⋯xrw​(𝝅)​(r).M_{G}(x_{1},\dots,x_{r},0,0,\dots)=\sum_{\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\mathop{\rm Max}\nolimits(\Pi_{G}^{r})}\mu_{\Pi_{G}^{r}}(\hat{0},\boldsymbol{\pi})x_{1}^{w(\boldsymbol{\pi})(1)}\cdots x_{r}^{w(\boldsymbol{\pi})(r)}.

For each rr, define the Möbius symmetric polynomial MG​(x1,…,xr)M_{G}(x_{1},\dots,x_{r}) in rr variables to be MG​(x1,…,xr,0,0,…)M_{G}(x_{1},\dots,x_{r},0,0,\dots).

Note that MG​(1)M_{G}(1) is the Möbius invariant μ⁡(ΠG)\mu(\Pi_{G}) of the bond lattice ΠG\Pi_{G} and MG​(1,t)M_{G}(1,t) is the Möbius polynomial μG​(t)\mu_{G}(t). From Figure 5.1, one can see that

MK3​(x1,x2,x3)=2​(x12+x22+x32)+5​(x1​x2+x1​x3+x2​x3)M_{K_{3}}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=2(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2})+5(x_{1}x_{2}+x_{1}x_{3}+x_{2}x_{3})

and from Figure 5.2, one can see that

MP3​(x1,x2,x3)=(x12+x22+x32)+3​(x1​x2+x1​x3+x2​x3).M_{P_{3}}(x_{1},x_{2},x_{3})=(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2}+x_{3}^{2})+3(x_{1}x_{2}+x_{1}x_{3}+x_{2}x_{3}).

The isomorphism given in Proposition 5.2 yields the following generalization of Proposition 2.2.

Proposition 5.4.

Let GG be a graph whose connected components are G1,…,GkG_{1},\dots,G_{k}. Then

MG​(𝐱)=∏i=1kMGi​(𝐱).M_{G}(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{i=1}^{k}M_{G_{i}}(\mathbf{x}).

5.3. Recurrence relations for Möbius symmetric functions

The recursive structure of the weighted partition poset is described in the following propositions, whose straightforward proofs are left to the reader. Recall the definitions of G|BG|B and G/πG/\pi given in Section 3.1. Equation (5.1) below is a consequence of the multiplicative property of the Möbius function (see [43, Proposition 3.8.2]).

Proposition 5.5.

Let GG be a graph and let r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}. If

𝝅={B1ν1,…,Bkνk}∈ΠGr,\boldsymbol{\pi}=\{B_{1}^{\nu_{1}},\dots,B_{k}^{\nu_{k}}\}\in\Pi_{G}^{r},

then

[0^,𝝅]G≅[0^,B1ν1]G|B1×⋯×[0^,Bkνk]G|Bk.[\hat{0},\boldsymbol{\pi}]_{G}\cong[\hat{0},B_{1}^{\nu_{1}}]_{G|_{B_{1}}}\times\cdots\times[\hat{0},B_{k}^{\nu_{k}}]_{G|_{B_{k}}}.

Consequently,

(5.1) μΠGr​(0^,𝝅)=∏i=1kμΠG|Bir​(0^,Biνi).\mu_{\Pi_{G}^{r}}(\hat{0},\boldsymbol{\pi})=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mu_{\Pi^{r}_{G|_{B_{i}}}}(\hat{0},B_{i}^{\nu_{i}}).

For 𝝅∈ΠGr\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\Pi^{r}_{G}, let UGr​(𝝅)U^{r}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\pi}) be the upper order ideal (order filter) generated by 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi}. For connected GG on vertex set VV and ν∈WComp|V|−1,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{|V|-1,r}, the maximal elements of UGr​(𝝅)U^{r}_{G}(\boldsymbol{\pi}) are of the form VνV^{\nu}, where

(5.2) ν−w⁡(𝝅)∈WComp|𝝅|−1,r.\nu-w(\boldsymbol{\pi})\in{\rm WComp}_{|\boldsymbol{\pi}|-1,r}.
Proposition 5.6.

5.4. Examples

In [22], González D’León uses the complete graph case of the recurrence relations of Theorem 5.7 to obtain the exponential generating function formula

∑n≥1MKn​(𝐱)​ynn!=(∑n≥1hn−1​(𝐱)​ynn!)⟨−1⟩,\sum_{n\geq 1}M_{K_{n}}(\mathbf{x})\frac{y^{n}}{n!}=\left(\sum_{n\geq 1}h_{n-1}(\mathbf{x})\dfrac{y^{n}}{n!}\right)^{\langle-1\rangle},

which is a symmetric function generalization of (3.3). In [22] it is shown that the coefficient of 𝐱ν\mathbf{x}^{\nu} in (−1)n−1​MKn​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-1}M_{K_{n}}(\mathbf{x}) is the dimension of a subspace of the multilineal component, associated with ν\nu, of the free Lie algebra with multiple compatible brackets.

The recurrence relations of Theorem 5.7 in the case of the star graph reduce to

∑k=0n−1(n−1k)​hk​(𝐱)​MS​tn−k​(𝐱)=δn,1.\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{k}h_{k}(\mathbf{x})\,M_{St_{n-k}}(\mathbf{x})=\delta_{n,1}.

This was used by González D’León [23] to obtain the exponential generating function formula

(5.5) ∑n≥0MS​tn+1​(𝐱)​ynn!=(∑n≥0hn​(𝐱)​ynn!)−1,\sum_{n\geq 0}M_{St_{n+1}}(\mathbf{x})\frac{y^{n}}{n!}=\left(\sum_{n\geq 0}h_{n}(\mathbf{x})\frac{y^{n}}{n!}\right)^{-1},

which is a symmetric function generalization of (3.10). It is shown in [23] that the coefficient of 𝐱ν\mathbf{x}^{\nu} in (−1)n−1​MS​tn​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-1}M_{St_{n}}(\mathbf{x}) is the dimension of a subspace of the multilinear component, associated with ν\nu, of the colored exterior algebra.

Remark 5.8.

The rr-weighted bond poset ΠS​tnr\Pi_{St_{n}}^{r} appeared in the guise of the rr-weighted Boolean algebra in the work of González D’León [23] on colored exterior algebras. For each 𝝅∈ΠS​tnr\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\Pi^{r}_{St_{n}}, let BνB^{\nu} be the weighted block of 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi} that contains 11. Now remove 11 from BB and reduce the remaining elements by 11 to get the set B¯\bar{B}. The map taking 𝝅\boldsymbol{\pi} to B¯ν\bar{B}^{\nu} defines an isomorphism from ΠS​tnr\Pi^{r}_{St_{n}} to the rr-weighted Boolean algebra consisting of weighted sets SνS^{\nu}, where S⊆[n−1]S\subseteq[n-1] and ν∈WComp|S|,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{|S|,r}. Note that in the r=2r=2 case, this rr-weighted Boolean algebra is a variant of the weighted Boolean algebra 𝒲​ℬn\mathcal{WB}_{n} mentioned in the Introduction.

Next we turn to the path graph PnP_{n}. By using the recurrence relations of Theorem 5.7, we will show that the Möbius symmetric functions for the path graphs are related to a class of symmetric functions known as parking function symmetric functions.

A parking function on [n][n] is a sequence (p1,…,pn)∈[n]n(p_{1},\dots,p_{n})\in[n]^{n} whose weakly increasing rearrangement pσ⁡(1)≤⋯≤pσ⁡(n)p_{\sigma(1)}\leq\cdots\leq p_{\sigma(n)} satisfies pσ⁡(i)≤ip_{\sigma(i)}\leq i for all i∈[n]i\in[n]; see [42, Exercise 5.49]. Let P​Fn​(𝐱)\mathnormal{PF}_{n}(\mathbf{x}) denote the Frobenius characteristic of the permutation representation associated with the action of 𝔖n\mathfrak{S}_{n} on the set of parking functions on [n][n], where a permutation acts by permuting the entries of the parking function. The symmetric function P​Fn​(𝐱)\mathnormal{PF}_{n}(\mathbf{x}) is known as the parking function symmetric function and was first considered in this context by Haiman [28]. In [41] Stanley observed that

(5.6) P​Fn​(𝐱)= coeff. of yn in ​1n+1​(∑j≥0hj​(𝐱)​yj)n+1.PF_{n}(\mathbf{x})=\mbox{ coeff. of $y^{n}$ in }\frac{1}{n+1}\left(\sum_{j\geq 0}h_{j}(\mathbf{x})y^{j}\right)^{n+1}.

Expansions of ω​P​Fn​(𝐱)\omega PF_{n}(\mathbf{x}) in the monomial symmetric function basis {mλ:λ⊢n}\{m_{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\} and in the elementary symmetric function basis {eλ:λ⊢n}\{e_{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\} can be found in [41] as well, where ω\omega is the involution on the ring of symmetric functions that takes hnh_{n} to ene_{n}. Given π∈Πn\pi\in\Pi_{n}, let λ⁡(π)\lambda(\pi) be the partition of nn given by

(5.7) λ⁡(π)=(|B1|,|B2|,…,|Bk|),\lambda(\pi)=(|B_{1}|,|B_{2}|,\dots,|B_{k}|),

where B1,…,BkB_{1},\dots,B_{k} are the blocks of π\pi listed in weakly decreasing order of size. For all n≥1n\geq 1,

(5.8) ω​P​Fn​(𝐱)=1n+1​∑λ⊢n∏i(n+1λ⁡(i))​mλ​(𝐱)\omega PF_{n}(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{\lambda\vdash n}\prod_{i}\binom{n+1}{\lambda(i)}m_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x})

and

(5.9) ω​P​Fn​(𝐱)=∑π∈𝒩​𝒞neλ⁡(π)​(𝐱),\omega PF_{n}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{NC}_{n}}e_{\lambda(\pi)}(\mathbf{x}),

where 𝒩​𝒞n\mathcal{NC}_{n} is the set of noncrossing partitions of [n][n].

Theorem 5.9.

For all n≥1n\geq 1,

(−1)n−1​MPn​(𝐱)=ω​P​Fn−1​(𝐱).(-1)^{n-1}M_{P_{n}}(\mathbf{x})=\omega PF_{n-1}(\mathbf{x}).
Proof.

The recurrence relations of Theorem 5.7 in the case of G=PnG=P_{n} reduce to

∑k=1nhk−1​(𝐱)​∑(n1,…,nk)⊨n∏i=1kMPni​(𝐱)=δn,1\sum_{k=1}^{n}h_{k-1}(\mathbf{x})\sum_{(n_{1},\dots,n_{k})\vDash n}\prod_{i=1}^{k}M_{P_{n_{i}}}(\mathbf{x})=\delta_{n,1}

and

∑k=1nMPk​(𝐱)​∑(n1,…,nk)⊨n∏i=1khni−1​(𝐱)=δn,1.\sum_{k=1}^{n}M_{P_{k}}(\mathbf{x})\sum_{(n_{1},\dots,n_{k})\vDash n}\prod_{i=1}^{k}h_{n_{i}-1}(\mathbf{x})=\delta_{n,1}.

Both equations are equivalent to the generating function formula

∑n≥1(−1)n−1​MPn​(𝐱)​yn=(∑n≥1(−1)n−1​hn−1​(𝐱)​yn)⟨−1⟩=(y∏i≥1(1+xi​y))⟨−1⟩,\sum_{n\geq 1}(-1)^{n-1}M_{P_{n}}(\mathbf{x})y^{n}=\left(\sum_{n\geq 1}(-1)^{n-1}h_{n-1}(\mathbf{x})\,y^{n}\right)^{\left\langle-1\right\rangle}=\left(\frac{y}{\prod_{i\geq 1}(1+x_{i}y)}\right)^{\left\langle-1\right\rangle},

1n​(∏i≥1(1+xi​y))n=1n​(∑j≥0ej​(𝐱)​yj)n.\frac{1}{n}\left(\prod_{i\geq 1}(1+x_{i}y)\right)^{n}=\frac{1}{n}\left(\sum_{j\geq 0}e_{j}(\mathbf{x})y^{j}\right)^{n}.
