We have the following consequence of Theorem 5.9 and Equation (5.8).

Corollary 5.10.

For all r,n≥1r,n\geq 1,

(−1)n−1MPn(x1,…,xr)=∑ν∈WCompn−1,r1n∏i=1r(nν⁡(i))x1ν⁡(1)⋯xrν⁡(r).(-1)^{n-1}M_{P_{n}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{r})=\sum_{\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r}}\frac{1}{n}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\binom{n}{\nu(i)}x_{1}^{\nu(1)}\cdots x_{r}^{\nu(r)}.

The coefficients Nν:=1n​∏i=1r(nν⁡(i))N_{\nu}:=\frac{1}{n}\prod_{i=1}^{r}\binom{n}{\nu(i)} are sometimes called generalized Fuss-Narayana numbers, in part, because they refine the Fuss-Narayana numbers Nr​(n,j):=1n​(nj)​((r−1)​nn−j−1)N_{r}(n,j):=\frac{1}{n}\binom{n}{j}\binom{(r-1)n}{n-j-1}, which in turn refine the Fuss-Catalan numbers Cn,r:=1n​(r​nn−1)C_{n,r}:=\frac{1}{n}\binom{rn}{n-1}. Indeed Vandermonde’s identity yields,

∑ν∈WCompn−1,rν⁡(r)=jNν=Nr​(n,j)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r}\\ \nu(r)=j\end{subarray}}N_{\nu}=N_{r}(n,j)

and

∑j=0n−1Nr​(n,j)=Cn,r.\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}N_{r}(n,j)=C_{n,r}.

It therefore follows from Corollary 5.10 that

(−1)n−1​MPn​(1,1,…,1⏞r)=Cn,r.(-1)^{n-1}M_{P_{n}}(\stackrel{{\scriptstyle r}}{{\overbrace{1,1,\dots,1}}})=C_{n,r}.

Note that Nr​(n,j)N_{r}(n,j) is the usual Narayana number N⁡(n,j)N(n,j) and Cn,rC_{n,r} is the usual Catalan number CnC_{n} when r=2r=2. Thus Corollary 5.10 reduces to Theorem 3.2 when r=2r=2.

Another consequence of Theorem 5.9 is that .(−1)n−1​MPn​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-1}M_{P_{n}}(\mathbf{x}) is ee-positive, that is when expanded in the basis of elementary symmetric functions, all the coefficients are nonnegative. Indeed, by (5.9),

(5.10) (−1)n−1​MPn​(𝐱)=∑π∈𝒩​𝒞n−1eλ⁡(π)​(𝐱).(-1)^{n-1}M_{P_{n}}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{NC}_{n-1}}e_{\lambda(\pi)}(\mathbf{x}).

In the next section we establish ee-positivity for all chordal graphs and conjecture that it holds for all graphs.

6. EL-shellability, ee-positivity, and γ\gamma-positivity

In this section, we prove ee-positivity results for the Möbius symmetric functions. These results reduce to the γ\gamma-positivity results for the Möbius polynomials discussed in Section 4.2. Our proofs rely on the theory of lexicographic shellability, which was first introduced by Björner in [9] and further devoloped by Björner and Wachs in [6, 7, 4, 5]. We briefly review the basics in Section 6.1. See [46] for further information on this topic.

6.1. Review: EL labeling of the multiweighted partition poset

An edge-labeling of a finite bounded poset PP is a function λ:ℰ⁡(P)→Λ\lambda:\mathcal{E}(P)\rightarrow\Lambda from the set ℰ⁡(P)\mathcal{E}(P) of cover relations of PP to some other poset Λ\Lambda. An edge labeling λ:ℰ⁡(P)→Λ\lambda:\mathcal{E}(P)\rightarrow\Lambda of PP is said to be an EL-labeling if it satisfies the following conditions:

  1. (1)

    In every closed interval [x,y][x,y] of PP there is a unique (strictly) increasing maximal chain, i.e., a maximal chain 𝐜:=(x=x0⋖x1⋖⋯⋖xℓ=y)\mathbf{c}:=(x=x_{0}\lessdot x_{1}\lessdot\cdots\lessdot x_{\ell}=y) such that

    λ⁡(x0⋖x1)<λ⁡(x1⋖x2)<⋯<λ⁡(xℓ−1⋖xℓ).\lambda(x_{0}\lessdot x_{1})<\lambda(x_{1}\lessdot x_{2})<\cdots<\lambda(x_{\ell-1}\lessdot x_{\ell}).
  2. (2)

    The word of labels

    λ(𝐜):=λ(x0⋖x1)λ(x1⋖x2)⋯λ(xℓ−1⋖xℓ)\lambda(\mathbf{c}):=\lambda(x_{0}\lessdot x_{1})\lambda(x_{1}\lessdot x_{2})\cdots\lambda(x_{\ell-1}\lessdot x_{\ell})

    associated to the unique increasing maximal chain 𝐜\mathbf{c} comes, in the lexicographic order, before the word of labels of any other maximal chain in the interval.

If PP admits an EL-labeling, we say that it is edge lexicographically shellable (EL-shellable). Note that the EL-labeling restricts to an EL-labeling of every closed interval of PP. A maximal chain x0⋖x1⋖⋯⋖xℓx_{0}\lessdot x_{1}\lessdot\cdots\lessdot x_{\ell} of a closed interval of PP is said to be ascent-free if its word of labels has no ascents, that is, for all i∈[ℓ−1]i\in[\ell-1] we have λ⁡(xi−1⋖xi)≮λ⁡(xi⋖xi+1)\lambda(x_{i-1}\lessdot x_{i})\not<\lambda(x_{i}\lessdot x_{i+1}).

For any maximal chain 𝐜\mathbf{c} of a closed interval [x,y][x,y], let 𝐜¯:=𝐜−{x,y}\bar{\mathbf{c}}:=\mathbf{c}-\{x,y\}. A chain x0<x1<⋯<xℓx_{0}<x_{1}<\cdots<x_{\ell} of length ℓ\ell in PP will be referred to as an ℓ\ell-chain.

EL-shellability has strong topological and algebraic implications for the order complex Δ⁡(x,y)\Delta(x,y) of each open interval (x,y)(x,y) of the poset. This will be discussed in Section 6.5, while here we only need its connection with the Möbius function as given in the following result.

Theorem 6.1 (Stanley [39], cf.​ Björner [9, Theorem 2.7]).

Let λ\lambda be an EL-labeling of a pure bounded finite poset PP. Then for every x≤Pyx\leq_{P}y in PP,

μ⁡(x,y)=(−1)ℓ⁡(x,y)​|{𝐜¯∣𝐜​ is an ascent-free maximal chain of ​[x,y]}|.\mu(x,y)=(-1)^{\ell(x,y)}|\{\bar{\mathbf{c}}\mid\mathbf{c}\text{ is an ascent-free maximal chain of }[x,y]\}|.
Remark 6.2.

This theorem is implicit in [39], where a less stringent labeling, now known as an ER-labeling (or R-labeling), was used. EL-shellabillity was introduced later in [9] in order to obtain stronger topological conclusions; see Theorem 6.27. In both papers the increasing maximal chains were only required to be weakly increasing and the ascents were defined as weak ascents. The theorem is valid either way; see [46, Remark 3.25].

Recall that the poset ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r} is pure, but not bounded. Hence we consider the augmented rr-weighted bond poset ΠGr^:=ΠGr∪{1^}\widehat{\Pi_{G}^{r}}:=\Pi_{G}^{r}\cup\{\hat{1}\}, which is pure and bounded. We now present an EL-labeling of ΠKnr^=Πnr^\widehat{\Pi_{K_{n}}^{r}}=\widehat{\Pi_{n}^{r}} obtained by González D’León and Wachs [20] in the r=2r=2 case and by González D’León [22] for general r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}. Note that the definition of EL-labeling makes sense not only for finite bounded posets, but also for infinite bounded posets in which all maximal chains are finite. Thus we can extend the definition of EL-labeling to such posets, which include the poset Πn∞^\widehat{\Pi_{n}^{\infty}}. Note also that all the closed intervals of Πn∞\Pi_{n}^{\infty} are finite. So the restriction of any EL-labeling of Πn∞^\widehat{\Pi_{n}^{\infty}} to any closed interval of Πn∞\Pi_{n}^{\infty} is an EL-labeling in the traditional sense.

For fixed r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\} and a∈[n]a\in[n], let

Γa,r={(a,b,j)∣a<b≤n+1​ and ​j∈[r]}\Gamma_{a,r}=\{(a,b,j)\mid a<b\leq n+1\text{ and }j\in[r]\}

with order relation given by (a,b,j)≤(a,b′,j′)(a,b,j)\leq(a,b^{\prime},j^{\prime}) whenever b≤b′b\leq b^{\prime} and j≤j′j\leq j^{\prime}. (Here [∞]:=ℤ>0[\infty]:=\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.) We define then Λn,r\Lambda_{n,r} as the ordinal sum

Λn,r=Γ1,r⊕Γ2,r⊕⋯⊕Γn,r.\Lambda_{n,r}=\Gamma_{1,r}\oplus\Gamma_{2,r}\oplus\cdots\oplus\Gamma_{n,r}.

See Figure 6.1 for the Hasse diagrams of Λ3,2\Lambda_{3,2} and Λ2,3\Lambda_{2,3}.

Recall that if 𝜶⋖𝜷\boldsymbol{\alpha}\lessdot\boldsymbol{\beta} in Πnr\Pi^{r}_{n} then 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} is obtained from 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} by merging two rr-weighted blocks AμA^{\mu} and BνB^{\nu} to obtain the rr-weighted block (A∪B)𝐞j+μ+ν(A\cup B)^{{\bf e}_{j}+\mu+\nu}, where j∈[r]j\in[r]. Assume min⁡A<min⁡B\min A<\min B and let

λ⁡(𝜶⋖𝜷)=(min⁡A,min⁡B,j).\lambda(\boldsymbol{\alpha}\lessdot\boldsymbol{\beta})=(\min A,\min B,j).

For all ν∈WCompn−1,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r}, let

λ⁡([n]ν⋖1^)=(1,n+1,1).\lambda([n]^{\nu}\lessdot\hat{1})=(1,n+1,1).

This defines an edge labeling λ:ℰ⁡(Πnr^)→Λn,r\lambda:\mathcal{E}(\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}})\to\Lambda_{n,r}.

Theorem 6.3 ([22], [20] r=2 case).

For all r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}, the edge labeling λ:ℰ⁡(Πnr^)→Λn,r\lambda:\mathcal{E}(\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}})\rightarrow\Lambda_{n,r} defined above is an EL-labeling of Πnr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}}.

Given any chain 𝐜{\bf c} of Πnr\Pi_{n}^{r}, the underlying partitions of the weighted partitions of 𝐜{\bf c} form a chain cc in Πn\Pi_{n}, which we call the underlying chain of 𝐜{\bf c}. We now describe the underlying chain of the unique increasing maximal chain of each interval of Πnr\Pi^{r}_{n} under the EL-labeling λ\lambda.

Definition 6.4.

Let α<β∈Πn\alpha<\beta\in\Pi_{n} and let

B1,…,BmB_{1},\dots,B_{m}

be the blocks of β\beta, listed in increasing order of their minimum elements. For each i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m, let

Ai,1,…,Ai,kiA_{i,1},\dots,A_{i,k_{i}}

be the blocks of α\alpha that are merged to form the block BiB_{i}, also listed in increasing order of their minimums. Now define the fundamental chain c⁡(α,β)c(\alpha,\beta) of the interval [α,β][\alpha,\beta] to be the concatenation of the chains c0,c1,…,cmc_{0},c_{1},\dots,c_{m}, where c0c_{0} is the chain consisting only of the partition α\alpha and for each i≥1i\geq 1, the chain cic_{i} is

(Ai,1∪Ai,2)⋖Πn(⋃j=13Ai,j)⋖Πn⋯⋖Πn(⋃j=1kiAi,j)=Bi,(A_{i,1}\cup A_{i,2})\lessdot_{\Pi_{n}}(\bigcup_{j=1}^{3}A_{i,j})\lessdot_{\Pi_{n}}\cdots\lessdot_{\Pi_{n}}(\bigcup_{j=1}^{k_{i}}A_{i,j})=B_{i},

where only the newly merged block is listed. In other words, cic_{i} is the chain

πi,1⋖Πnπi,2⋖Πn⋯⋖Πnπi,ki−1\pi_{i,1}\lessdot_{\Pi_{n}}\pi_{i,2}\lessdot_{\Pi_{n}}\cdots\lessdot_{\Pi_{n}}\pi_{i,k_{i}-1}

where for each p∈[ki−1]p\in[k_{i}-1], the partition πi,p\pi_{i,p} is equal to

{B1,…,Bi−1}∪{⋃j=1p+1Ai,j,Ai,p+2,…,Ai,ki}∪⋃j=i+1m{Aj,1,…,Aj,kj}.\{B_{1},\dots,B_{i-1}\}\cup\{\bigcup_{j=1}^{p+1}A_{i,j},A_{i,p+2},\dots,A_{i,k_{i}}\}\cup\bigcup_{j=i+1}^{m}\{A_{j,1},\dots,A_{j,k_{j}}\}.

The following result is extracted from the proof of Theorem 6.3 given in [22, 20].

Lemma 6.5.

Let 𝛂<𝛃∈Πnr^\boldsymbol{\alpha}<\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}}.

  1. (1)

    If 𝜷≠1^\boldsymbol{\beta}\neq\hat{1} then the underlying chain of the unique increasing maximal chain of [𝜶,𝜷][\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}] is the fundamental chain c⁡(α,β)c(\alpha,\beta), where α\alpha is the underlying partition of 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} and β\beta is the underlying partition of 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta}.

  2. (2)

    Suppose 𝜷=1^\boldsymbol{\beta}=\hat{1}. Then the unique increasing maximal chain of [𝜶,𝜷][\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}] is the concatenation of the unique increasing maximal chain of [𝜶,[n]w⁡(𝜶)+(|𝜶|−1)​𝐞1][\boldsymbol{\alpha},[n]^{w(\boldsymbol{\alpha})+(|\boldsymbol{\alpha}|-1){\bf e}_{1}}] and 1^\hat{1}, where w⁡(𝜶)w(\boldsymbol{\alpha}) is the sum of the weights of the blocks of 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha}.

6.2. Review: Lyndon-colored trees and ascent-free chains

In this section we present the description given in [22, 20] of the ascent-free maximal chains of each maximal interval [0^,[n]ν][\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}] of Πnr\Pi_{n}^{r} under the EL-labeling λ\lambda of Theorem 6.3 in terms of certain leaf labeled binary trees with colored internal nodes. This, by Corollary 6.1, gives a combinatorial description of the coefficients of the Möbius symmetric function.

Recall that for each rr, each maximal interval [0^,[n]ν][\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}] of Πnr\Pi_{n}^{r} can be viewed as a maximal interval of Πn∞\Pi_{n}^{\infty} by viewing the weak rr-compositions as weak ∞\infty-compositions. Hence we can restrict ourselves to r=∞r=\infty in what follows.

Recall the discussion of leaf-labeled binary trees given in Section 4.2. Now we add color to the internal nodes of these trees. Let 𝐢𝐧𝐭(T){\bf\mathop{int}}(T) be the set of internal nodes of a binary tree TT. A coloring of a binary tree TT is a function 𝐜𝐥𝐫:𝐢𝐧𝐭(T)→ℤ>0{\bf\mathop{clr}}:{\bf\mathop{int}}(T)\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}_{>0} that assigns a positive integer or color to every internal node of TT. For each colored leaf-labeled binary tree TT, define the color type of TT to be the weak ∞\infty-composition ν⁡(T)=(ν⁡(1),ν⁡(2),⋯)\nu(T)=(\nu(1),\nu(2),\cdots), where ν⁡(i)\nu(i) is the number of internal nodes of TT that have color ii. For each ν∈WCompn−1\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1}, let 𝒞​𝒯n,ν\mathcal{CT}_{n,\nu} denote the set of colored binary trees on leaf set [n][n] that have color type ν\nu.

Recall the discussion of normalized leaf-labeled binary tree and Lyndon nodes in Section 4.2. A Lyndon-coloring of a normalized leaf-labeled binary tree TT is a coloring 𝐜𝐥𝐫{\bf\mathop{clr}} that satisfies: for all internal nodes xx of TT whose left child L⁡(x)L(x) is not a leaf,

min⁡AR⁡(L⁡(x))<min⁡AR⁡(x)⟹𝐜𝐥𝐫(L⁡(x))>𝐜𝐥𝐫(x).\min A_{R(L(x))}<\min A_{R(x)}\implies{\bf\mathop{clr}}(L(x))>{\bf\mathop{clr}}(x).

In other words, each nonLyndon internal node must be assigned a color that is less than the color assigned to its left child. Thus only Lyndon trees can have a monochromatic Lyndon-coloring. For ν∈WCompn−1\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1}, let ℒ​y​nn,ν\mathcal{L}yn_{n,\nu} denote the set of Lyndon-colored normalized binary trees on leaf set [n][n] that have color type ν\nu.

An example of a Lyndon-colored normalized binary tree in ℒ​y​n6,(2,2,1)\mathcal{L}yn_{6,(2,2,1)} is given in Figure 6.2. The small number next to each internal node xx is min⁡Ax\min A_{x} and the circled numbers give an ordering of the internal nodes which will be explained below. In Figure 6.3, all the Lyndon-colored normalized binary trees on leaf set [3][3] with colors in [2][2] are listed. From this we see that

|ℒ​y​n3,(2,0)|=2​ and ​|ℒ​y​n3,(1,1)|=5​ and ​|ℒ​y​n3,(0,2)|=2|\mathcal{L}yn_{3,(2,0)}|=2\,\,\mbox{ and }\,\,|\mathcal{L}yn_{3,(1,1)}|=5\,\,\mbox{ and }\,\,|\mathcal{L}yn_{3,(0,2)}|=2

Binary trees on leaf set [n][n] are used in [45] to encode maximal chains of Πn=Πn1\Pi_{n}=\Pi_{n}^{1} and bicolored binary trees on leaf set [n][n] are used in [20] to encode maximal chains of 𝒲​Πn=Πn2\mathcal{W}\Pi_{n}=\Pi_{n}^{2}. The general rr-colored binary trees on leaf set [n][n] are used in [22] to encode maximal chains of Πnr\Pi_{n}^{r}. Now we describe how this is done.

We call an ordering of the internal nodes of a binary tree TT in which each node appears before its parent, a linear extension of TT. For each 𝐓∈𝒞​𝒯n,ν\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{CT}_{n,\nu} and linear extension τ=(x1,…,xn−1)\tau=(x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}) of 𝐓\mathbf{T}, we can construct a maximal chain

c⁡(𝐓,τ)=(0^=𝝅0⋖𝝅1⋖⋯⋖𝝅n−1=[n]ν)c(\mathbf{T},\tau)=(\hat{0}=\boldsymbol{\pi}_{0}\lessdot\boldsymbol{\pi}_{1}\lessdot\cdots\lessdot\boldsymbol{\pi}_{n-1}=[n]^{\nu})

of [0^,[n]ν][\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}] such that for all i∈[n−1]i\in[n-1], the weighted partition 𝝅i\boldsymbol{\pi}_{i} is obtained from the weighted partition 𝝅i−1\boldsymbol{\pi}_{i-1} by merging the weighted blocks AL⁡(xi)αA_{L(x_{i})}^{\alpha} and AR⁡(xi)βA_{R(x_{i})}^{\beta} of 𝝅i−1\boldsymbol{\pi}_{i-1} to obtain the weighted block Axiα+β+𝐞𝐜𝐥𝐫(xi)A_{x_{i}}^{\alpha+\beta+{\bf e}_{{\bf\mathop{clr}}(x_{i})}} of 𝝅i\boldsymbol{\pi}_{i}. In Figure 6.4 we illustrate the chain c⁡(𝐓,τ)c(\mathbf{T},\tau) associated to the colored leaf-labeled tree 𝐓\mathbf{T} of Figure 6.2 and the linear extension τ\tau given by the circled numbers.

Note that every maximal chain of [0^,[n]ν][\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}] can be represented as c⁡(𝐓,τ)c(\mathbf{T},\tau) for some 𝐓∈𝒞​𝒯n,ν\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{CT}_{n,\nu} and linear extension τ\tau of 𝐓\mathbf{T}. However, the pair (𝐓,τ)(\mathbf{T},\tau) is not unique unless we restrict to normalized trees in 𝒞​𝒯n,ν\mathcal{CT}_{n,\nu}. It is not difficult to see that for each binary tree TT on leaf set [n][n], there is a unique linear extension (x1,…,xn−1)(x_{1},\dots,x_{n-1}) of TT such that

min⁡Ax1≥min⁡Ax2≥⋯≥min⁡Axn−1.\min A_{x_{1}}\geq\min A_{x_{2}}\geq\cdots\geq\min A_{x_{n-1}}.

We will call this linear extension the decreasing-minimum linear extension of TT and denote it by τT\tau_{T}. The linear extension depicted by the circled numbers in Figure 6.2 is the decreasing-minimum linear extension τT\tau_{T} of the colored tree TT in the figure.

Theorem 6.6 ([22], r=2 case [20]).

For all ν∈WCompn−1,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r},

{c⁡(𝐓,τ𝐓)∣𝐓∈ℒ​y​nn,ν}\{c(\mathbf{T},\tau_{\mathbf{T}})\mid\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{n,\nu}\}

is the set of ascent-free maximal chains of the interval [0^,[n]ν][\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}] under the EL-labeling of Πn∞^\widehat{\Pi_{n}^{\infty}} given inTheorem 6.3.

Now by Corollary 6.1, we have the following result.

Corollary 6.7 ([22]).

For all n≥1n\geq 1,

(−1)n−1​MKn​(𝐱)=∑ν∈WCompn−1|ℒ​y​nn,ν|​𝐱ν.(-1)^{n-1}M_{K_{n}}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1}}|\mathcal{L}yn_{n,\nu}|\mathbf{x}^{\nu}.

From this corollary, one can show that (−1)n−1​MKn​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-1}M_{K_{n}}(\mathbf{x}) is ee-positive. Details are given in a more general setting in Section 6.3. From Figure 6.3, one can see that

MK3​(x1,x2)=2​x12+5​x1​x2+2​x22=e2​(x1,x2)+2​e1,1​(x1,x2)M_{K_{3}}(x_{1},x_{2})=2x_{1}^{2}+5x_{1}x_{2}+2x_{2}^{2}=e_{2}(x_{1},x_{2})+2e_{1,1}(x_{1},x_{2})

6.3. Generalization to chordal graphs

In this section, we generalize the results of the previous section to multiweighted bond posets of chordal graphs.

Recall the definitions of PEO and perfectly labeled chordal graph from Section 4. The following observation gives an equivalent definition of a PEO.

Proposition 6.8.

An ordering v1,v2,⋯,vnv_{1},v_{2},\cdots,v_{n} of the vertices of a graph GG is a PEO if and only if whenever i<j<ki<j<k, and {vi,vk}\{v_{i},v_{k}\} and {vj,vk}\{v_{j},v_{k}\} are edges of GG then {vi,vj}\{v_{i},v_{j}\} must also be an edge of GG, i.e., there are no induced subgraphs that are paths of the form vi−vk−vjv_{i}-v_{k}-v_{j}.

Corollary 6.9.

Let GG be a perfectly labeled chordal graph and let HH be an induced subgraph. Then HH is a perfectly labeled chordal graph.

Let GG be a graph on vertex set {v1<⋯<vn}⊆ℤ>0\{v_{1}<\dots<v_{n}\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{>0}. We say that a sequence vj1,vj2,…,vjmv_{j_{1}},v_{j_{2}},\dots,v_{j_{m}} is an increasing path from vj1v_{j_{1}} to vjmv_{j_{m}} if j1<j2<⋯<jmj_{1}<j_{2}<\dots<j_{m} and {vji,vji+1}\{v_{j_{i}},v_{j_{i+1}}\} is an edge of GG for all i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1].

Lemma 6.10.

Let GG be a connected perfectly labeled chordal graph on vertex set {v1<⋯<vn}⊆ℤ>0\{v_{1}<\dots<v_{n}\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{>0}. Then for any j∈[n]j\in[n] there is an increasing path from v1v_{1} to vjv_{j}.

Proof.

Using the fact that any induced subgraph of a perfectly labeled chordal graph is a perfectly labeled chordal graph (Corollary 6.9), we will proceed by induction on the number nn of vertices of GG. In graphs with one vertex the statement is trivial, so we assume that the lemma is true for any graph with less than nn vertices and let GG be a graph with nn vertices. Suppose there are no increasing paths from v1v_{1} to vjv_{j}. Note then in particular, j>1j>1 and {v1,vj}\{v_{1},v_{j}\} cannot be an edge of GG. If the graph G−{vj}G-\{v_{j}\} has more than one component, we can consider the induced subgraph formed by vjv_{j} and the component of G−{vj}G-\{v_{j}\} that contains v1v_{1}. Since this is a connected graph with less than nn vertices, we will find an increasing path from v1v_{1} to vjv_{j}, which gives a contradiction. This implies that G−{vj}G-\{v_{j}\} has to be connected.

Let vkv_{k} be the neighbor of vjv_{j} in GG with kk as small as possible. We know that k>1k>1 but it must happen that k>jk>j, otherwise if k<jk<j we could find an increasing path pp from v1v_{1} to vkv_{k} in G−{vj}G-\{v_{j}\} and then pp concatenated with vjv_{j} is an increasing path from v1v_{1} to vjv_{j} in GG. So let now pp be an increasing path in G−{vj}G-\{v_{j}\} from v1v_{1} to vkv_{k} and let {vi,vk}\{v_{i},v_{k}\} be its last edge. Since pp is increasing i<ki<k. Taking into account the minimality of kk, the vertices vi,vj,vkv_{i},v_{j},v_{k} provide a violation to the condition of a PEO given in Proposition 6.8, which gives us a contradiction. Hence there must be an increasing path from v1v_{1} to vjv_{j} for all j∈[n]j\in[n]. ∎

We will need the following lemma to prove that rr-weighted bond posets of chordal graphs are EL-shellable.

Lemma 6.11.

Let GG be a connected perfectly labeled chordal graph on [n][n]. Let B1,B2,…,BkB_{1},B_{2},\dots,B_{k} be a collection of disjoint subsets of [n][n] such that

  • •

    min⁡B1<min⁡B2<⋯<min⁡Bk\min B_{1}<\min B_{2}<\cdots<\min B_{k}

  • •

    G|BjG|_{B_{j}} is connected for all jj

  • •

    G|B1∪B2∪⋯∪BkG|_{B_{1}\cup B_{2}\cup\cdots\cup B_{k}} is connected.

Then for every s≤ks\leq k, the subgraph G|B1∪B2∪⋯∪BsG|_{B_{1}\cup B_{2}\cup\cdots\cup B_{s}} is connected.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on ss. If s=1s=1 we have from the hypothesis that G|B1G|_{B_{1}} is connected; so let us assume that G|B1∪B2∪⋯∪Bs−1G|_{B_{1}\cup B_{2}\cup\cdots\cup B_{s-1}} is connected. Since G|B1∪B2∪⋯∪BkG|_{B_{1}\cup B_{2}\cup\cdots\cup B_{k}} is connected we know from Corollary 6.9 and Lemma 6.10 that there is an increasing path pp from min⁡B1\min B_{1} to min⁡Bs\min B_{s}. Let {j,min⁡Bs}\{j,\min B_{s}\} be the last edge of pp. Since pp is increasing we have that j<min⁡Bsj<\min B_{s} and hence, by the fact that the BiB_{i}’s are listed in increasing order of their minimums, we have that j∈B1∪⋯∪Bs−1j\in B_{1}\cup\cdots\cup B_{s-1}. Hence G|B1∪⋯∪BsG|_{B_{1}\cup\cdots\cup B_{s}} is connected. ∎

We are now ready to prove that the augmented rr-weighted bond posets of chordal graphs are EL-shellable. Let GG be a connected graph on [n][n] and r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}. Note that each maximal chain of ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}} is a maximal chain of Πnr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}}. Hence any edge labeling of Πnr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}} can be restricted to an edge labeling of ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}}.

Theorem 6.12.

Let GG be a connected perfectly labeled chordal graph on [n][n] and let r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}. Then the restriction to ℰ⁡(ΠGr^)\mathcal{E}(\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}}) of the EL labeling λ:ℰ⁡(Πnr^)→Λn,r\lambda:\mathcal{E}(\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}})\to\Lambda_{n,r} given in Theorem 6.3 is an EL-labeling of ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}}.

Proof.

Let 𝜶<𝜷\boldsymbol{\alpha}<\boldsymbol{\beta} in ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}}. One need only show that the unique increasing maximal chain of the interval [𝜶,𝜷][\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}] in Πnr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}} is also a chain ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}}. The result will then follow from Theorem 6.3.

Suppose 𝜷≠1^\boldsymbol{\beta}\neq\hat{1} and let α\alpha and β\beta be the underlying partitions of 𝜶\boldsymbol{\alpha} and 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta}, respectively. Let Ai,jA_{i,j}, 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m, 1≤j≤ki1\leq j\leq k_{i}, be as in Definition 6.4. Since α,β∈ΠG\alpha,\beta\in\Pi_{G}, each induced subgraph G|Ai,jG|_{A_{i,j}} is connected as is G|⋃j=1kiAi,jG|_{\bigcup_{j=1}^{k_{i}}A_{i,j}}. It therefore follows from Lemma 6.11 that the induced subgraph G|⋃j=1sAi,jG|_{\bigcup_{j=1}^{s}A_{i,j}} is connected for all i=1,…,mi=1,\dots,m and s=1,…,kis=1,\dots,k_{i}. Hence, the chains cic_{i} of Definition 6.4 are in ΠG\Pi_{G}, which means that the fundamental chain c⁡(α,β)c(\alpha,\beta) of [α,β][\alpha,\beta] (i.e, the concatenation of c0,c1,…,cmc_{0},c_{1},\dots,c_{m}) is as well. Now by Lemma 6.5 (1), the unique increasing maximal chain of the interval [𝜶,𝜷][\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}] of Πnr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}} is also a chain in ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}}.

Now suppose β=1^\beta=\hat{1}. Let ν∈WCompn−1,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r} and let 𝐜ν{\bf c}_{\nu} be the unique increasing maximal chain of [𝜶,[n]ν][\boldsymbol{\alpha},[n]^{\nu}] in Πnr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}}. By the previous case, 𝐜ν{\mathbf{c}}_{\nu} is also in ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}}. Hence so is the concatenation of 𝐜ν{\bf c}_{\nu} with 1^\hat{1}. This means that the unique increasing maximal chain of [𝜶,𝜷][\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}] in Πnr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{n}}, as identified by Lemma 6.5 (2), is also in ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}}. ∎

Corollary 6.13.

If GG is a chordal graph then all closed intervals of ΠGr\Pi^{r}_{G} are EL-shellable for all r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}.

Proof.

We only need to prove this for maximal closed intervals. Since GG is chordal, its connected components G1,…,GkG_{1},\dots,G_{k} are chordal as well. Since every chordal graph can be perfectly labeled, each ΠGir^\widehat{\Pi_{G_{i}}^{r}} is EL-shellable by Theorem 6.12. It follows that each maximal closed interval of ΠGir\Pi^{r}_{G_{i}} is EL-shellable. By Proposition 5.2 each maximal closed interval of ΠGr\Pi^{r}_{G} is isomorphic to a product P1×⋯×PkP_{1}\times\cdots\times P_{k}, where each PiP_{i} is a maximal closed interval of ΠGir\Pi^{r}_{G_{i}}. The result now follows from [9, Theorem 4.3]. ∎

Question 6.14.

Is ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}} EL-shellable for every graph GG and for all r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}?

We have the following generalization of Theorem 6.6.

Theorem 6.15.

Let GG be a connected perfectly labeled chordal graph on [n][n] and let ν∈WCompn−1\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1}. Then the set of ascent-free maximal chains of the interval [0^,[n]ν]G[\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}]_{G} for the EL-labeling of ΠG∞^\widehat{\Pi^{\infty}_{G}} given in Theorem 6.12 is

{c⁡(𝐓,τT)∣𝐓∈ℒ​y​nG,ν},\{c(\mathbf{T},\tau_{T})\mid\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}\},

where

ℒ​y​nG,ν:={𝐓∈ℒ​y​nn,ν:G|Ax​ is connected for all nodes x of 𝐓}.\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}:=\{\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{n,\nu}:G|_{A_{x}}\mbox{ is connected for all nodes $x$ of $\mathbf{T}$}\}.
Proof.

Since the EL-labeling of ΠG∞^\widehat{\Pi^{\infty}_{G}} is the restriction of the EL-labeling of ΠKn∞^\widehat{\Pi^{\infty}_{K_{n}}}, the ascent-free chains of any interval [𝜶,𝜷][\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}] of ΠG∞^\widehat{\Pi^{\infty}_{G}} are the ascent-free chains of the interval [𝜶,𝜷][\boldsymbol{\alpha},\boldsymbol{\beta}] of ΠKn∞^\widehat{\Pi^{\infty}_{K_{n}}} that are also in ΠG∞^\widehat{\Pi^{\infty}_{G}}. The ascent-free maximal chains of the interval [0^,[n]ν]Kn[\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}]_{K_{n}}, as given in Theorem 6.6, have the form c⁡(𝐓,τT)c(\mathbf{T},\tau_{T}), where 𝐓∈ℒ​y​nn,ν\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{n,\nu}. Clearly, the chain c⁡(𝐓,τ𝐓)c(\mathbf{T},\tau_{\mathbf{T}}) is in ΠG∞^\widehat{\Pi^{\infty}_{G}} if and only if G|AxG|_{A_{x}} is connected for all nodes xx of 𝐓\mathbf{T}. Thus the ascent-free chains of [0^,[n]ν][\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}] are precisely the chains c⁡(𝐓,τ𝐓)c(\mathbf{T},\tau_{\mathbf{T}}) for which 𝐓∈ℒ​y​nG,ν\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}. ∎

Now by Corollary 6.1 we have the following consequence.

Corollary 6.16.

Let GG be a connected perfectly labeled chordal graph on [n][n]. Then

(−1)n−1​MG​(𝐱)=∑ν∈WComp⁡(n−1)|ℒ​y​nG,ν|​𝐱ν.(-1)^{n-1}M_{G}({\bf x})=\sum_{\nu\in{\rm WComp}(n-1)}|\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}|{\bf x}^{\nu}.
Example 6.17.

For G=P3G=P_{3}, the only trees of Figure 6.3 that are in ℒ​y​nG,ν\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu} for some ν\nu are the ones in the first row. Hence by Corollary 6.16,

MP3​(x1,x2)=x12+3​x1​x2+x22=e2​(x1,x2)+e1,1​(x1,x2).M_{P_{3}}(x_{1},x_{2})=x_{1}^{2}+3x_{1}x_{2}+x_{2}^{2}=e_{2}(x_{1},x_{2})+e_{1,1}(x_{1},x_{2}).

Given a normalized binary tree TT on node set [n][n], define the Lyndon set partition π⁡(T)\pi(T) to be the finest partition of the set 𝐢𝐧𝐭(T){\bf\mathop{int}}(T) that satisfies if x∈𝐢𝐧𝐭(T)x\in{\bf\mathop{int}}(T) is not a Lyndon node, then xx and L⁡(x)L(x) are in the same block of π\pi. The Lyndon type λ⁡(T)\lambda(T) of TT is the partition of n−1n-1 whose parts are the sizes of the blocks of the Lyndon set partition π⁡(T)\pi(T); that is

(6.1) λ⁡(T)=λ⁡(π⁡(T)),\lambda(T)=\lambda(\pi(T)),

where λ⁡(π)\lambda(\pi) is the number partition associated with the set partition π\pi, as in (5.7). For example, for the tree TT of Figure 6.2 (with colors ignored) we have that λ⁡(T)=(2,1,1,1)\lambda(T)=(2,1,1,1).

Theorem 6.18.

Let GG be a connected perfectly labeled chordal graph on [n][n]. Then

(−1)n−1​MG​(𝐱)=∑T∈𝒩Geλ⁡(T)​(𝐱),(-1)^{n-1}M_{G}({\bf x})=\sum_{T\in\mathcal{N}_{G}}e_{\lambda(T)}(\mathbf{x}),

where 𝒩G\mathcal{N}_{G} is the set of normalized binary trees TT on leaf set [n][n] for which G|AxG|_{A_{x}} is connected for all nodes xx of TT.

Consequently, if GG is a connected chordal graph then (−1)n−1​MG​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-1}M_{G}({\bf x}) is ee-positive.

Proof.

Let T∈𝒩GT\in\mathcal{N}_{G}. Each block of π⁡(T)\pi(T) forms a path y1,y2,…,yky_{1},y_{2},\dots,y_{k} of internal nodes of TT such that for each i∈[k−1]i\in[k-1], L⁡(yi)=yi+1L(y_{i})=y_{i+1} and yiy_{i} is nonLyndon. It follows that a coloring map 𝐜𝐥𝐫:𝐢𝐧𝐭(T)→ℤ>0{\bf\mathop{clr}}:{\bf\mathop{int}}(T)\to\mathbb{Z}_{>0} is a Lyndon-coloring if and only if

𝐜𝐥𝐫(y1)<𝐜𝐥𝐫(y2)<⋯<𝐜𝐥𝐫(yk){\bf\mathop{clr}}(y_{1})<{\bf\mathop{clr}}(y_{2})<\dots<{\bf\mathop{clr}}(y_{k})

for all blocks.

Hence,

(6.2) ∑𝐓∈ℒ​y​nG𝐓=(T,𝐜𝐥𝐫)𝐱ν⁡(𝐓)=eλ⁡(T)​(𝐱),\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{G}\\ {\bf T}=(T,{\bf\mathop{clr}})\end{subarray}}{\bf x}^{\nu({\bf T})}=e_{\lambda(T)}({\bf x}),

where

ℒ​y​nG:=⋃ν∈WCompn−1ℒ​y​nG,ν\mathcal{L}yn_{G}:=\bigcup_{\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1}}\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}

and TT is the underlying uncolored tree of 𝐓{\bf T}.

From Corollary 6.16 and Equation (6.2) we have

(−1)n−1​MG​(𝐱)\displaystyle(-1)^{n-1}M_{G}({\bf x}) =∑ν∈WCompn−1|ℒ​y​nG,ν|​𝐱ν\displaystyle=\sum_{\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1}}|\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}|\mathbf{x}^{\nu}
=∑𝐓∈ℒ​y​nG𝐱ν⁡(𝐓)\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{G}}\mathbf{x}^{\nu(\mathbf{T})}
=∑T∈𝒩G∑𝐓∈ℒ​y​nG𝐓=(T,𝐜𝐥𝐫)𝐱ν⁡(𝐓)\displaystyle=\sum_{T\in\mathcal{N}_{G}}\,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{G}\\ {\bf T}=(T,{\bf\mathop{clr}})\end{subarray}}{\bf x}^{\nu({\bf T})}
=∑T∈𝒩Geλ⁡(T)​(𝐱).\displaystyle=\sum_{T\in\mathcal{N}_{G}}\,e_{\lambda(T)}(\mathbf{x}).

∎

Proof of Theorem 4.4.

This is a special case of Theorem 6.18. Indeed, we use the facts that μG​(t)=MG​(1,t)\mu_{G}(t)=M_{G}(1,t) and

eλ​(1,t)={tm2​(λ)​(1+t)m1​(λ) if λ has no parts greater than 20 otherwise,e_{\lambda}(1,t)=\begin{cases}t^{m_{2}(\lambda)}(1+t)^{m_{1}(\lambda)}&\mbox{ if $\lambda$ has no parts greater than $2$}\\ 0&\mbox{ otherwise,}\end{cases}

where mi​(λ)m_{i}(\lambda) is the number of parts of λ\lambda that are equal to ii. Clearly for T∈𝒩GT\in\mathcal{N}_{G}, the partition λ⁡(T)\lambda(T) has no parts greater than 22 if and only if T∈𝒩G^T\in\widehat{\mathcal{N}_{G}}. In this case m2​(λ​(T))m_{2}(\lambda(T)) equals the number m⁡(T)m(T) of nonLyndon nodes of TT and m1​(λ⁡(T))=n−1−2​m2​(λ⁡(T)).m_{1}(\lambda(T))=n-1-2m_{2}(\lambda(T)). Hence the result follows from Theorem 6.18. ∎

Corollary 6.19.

Let GG be a chordal graph with nn vertices and kk connected components. Then the symmetric function (−1)n−k​MG​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-k}M_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is ee-positive.

Proof.

This follows from Theorem 6.18, Proposition 5.4, and the fact that products of ee-positive symmetric functions are ee-positive. ∎

Corollary 6.20.

Let GG and HH be perfectly labeled chordal graphs with nn vertices and kk connected components. If HH is a subgraph of GG then

(−1)n−k​(MG​(𝐱)−MH​(𝐱))(-1)^{n-k}(M_{G}({\mathbf{x}})-M_{H}({\mathbf{x}}))

is ee-positive.

Proof.

Suppose GG is connected. Then HH must be as well since it has the same number of connected components as GG. Clearly 𝒩H⊆𝒩G\mathcal{N}_{H}\subseteq\mathcal{N}_{G}. Hence by Theorem 6.18

(−1)n−1​(MG​(𝐱)−MH​(𝐱))=∑T∈𝒩G−𝒩Heλ⁡(T)​(𝐱).(-1)^{n-1}(M_{G}({\mathbf{x}})-M_{H}({\mathbf{x}}))=\sum_{T\in\mathcal{N}_{G}-\mathcal{N}_{H}}e_{\lambda(T)}(\mathbf{x}).

Now suppose GG has connected components Gi=(Vi,Ei)G_{i}=(V_{i},E_{i}), where i∈[k]i\in[k]. Then HH must have connected components Hi=(Vi,Ei′)H_{i}=(V_{i},E_{i}^{\prime}) where Ei′⊆EiE_{i}^{\prime}\subseteq E_{i}. It follows from Theorem 6.18 and Corollary 6.20 in the connected case that all (−1)|Vi|−1​MGi​(𝐱)(-1)^{|V_{i}|-1}M_{G_{i}}({\mathbf{x}}), (−1)|Vi|−1​MHi​(𝐱)(-1)^{|V_{i}|-1}M_{H_{i}}({\mathbf{x}}), and (−1)|Vi|−1​(MGi​(𝐱)−MHi​(𝐱))(-1)^{|V_{i}|-1}(M_{G_{i}}({\mathbf{x}})-M_{H_{i}}({\mathbf{x}})) are ee-positive. By Proposition 5.4,

(−1)n−k​(MG​(𝐱)−MH​(𝐱))=∏i=1k(−1)|Vi|−1​MGi​(𝐱)−∏i=1k(−1)|Vi|−1​MHi​(𝐱).(-1)^{n-k}(M_{G}({\mathbf{x}})-M_{H}(\mathbf{x}))=\prod_{i=1}^{k}(-1)^{|V_{i}|-1}M_{G_{i}}({\mathbf{x}})-\prod_{i=1}^{k}(-1)^{|V_{i}|-1}M_{H_{i}}({\mathbf{x}}).

We now use the fact that if fi,gif_{i},g_{i}, where i∈[k]i\in[k], are symmetric functions and the fif_{i}’s, gig_{i}’s and fi−gif_{i}-g_{i}’s are ee-positive then ∏i=1kfi−∏i=1kgi\prod_{i=1}^{k}f_{i}-\prod_{i=1}^{k}g_{i} is ee-positive. This follows by induction from the k=2k=2 case, which holds because

f1​f2−g1​g2=(f1−g1)​f2+(f2−g2)​g1f_{1}f_{2}-g_{1}g_{2}=(f_{1}-g_{1})f_{2}+(f_{2}-g_{2})g_{1}

and products and sums of ee-positive symmetric functions are ee-positive. Thus (−1)n−k​(MG​(𝐱)−MH​(𝐱))(-1)^{n-k}(M_{G}({\mathbf{x}})-M_{H}(\mathbf{x})) is ee-positive. ∎

Conjecture 6.21.

Let GG be a graph with nn vertices and kk connected components. Then

  1. (1)

    (−1)n−k​MG​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-k}M_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is ee-positive.

  2. (2)

    If HH is a subgraph of GG with nn vertices and kk connected components then

    (−1)n−k​(MG​(𝐱)−MH​(𝐱))(-1)^{n-k}(M_{G}({\mathbf{x}})-M_{H}({\mathbf{x}}))

    is ee-positive.

We have verified (1) for this conjecture computationally for all graphs with up to 77 vertices.

6.4. Examples

Let 𝒰​𝒯n,r\mathcal{UT}_{n,r} denote the set of unlabeled (i.e. no leaf labels) rr-ary trees with nn internal nodes. For each ν∈WCompn,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n,r}, let 𝒰​𝒯ν,r\mathcal{UT}_{\nu,r} be the set of rr-ary planar trees TT such that, for each ii, ν⁡(i)\nu(i) is the number of internal nodes of TT whose iith child (from left to right) is an internal node.

Theorem 6.22.

For all r,n≥1r,n\geq 1,

(−1)n−1MPn(x1,…,xr)=∑ν∈WCompn,r|𝒰𝒯ν,r|x1ν⁡(1)⋯xrν⁡(r).(-1)^{n-1}M_{P_{n}}(x_{1},\dots,x_{r})=\sum_{\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n,r}}|\mathcal{UT}_{\nu,r}|\,\,x_{1}^{\nu(1)}\cdots x_{r}^{\nu(r)}.
Proof.

For any graph GG on [n][n], let ℒ​y​nG,r=⋃ν∈WCompn−1,rℒ​y​nG,ν\mathcal{L}yn_{G,r}=\bigcup_{\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r}}\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}. The result follows from Corollary 6.16 and the direct bijection between ℒ​y​nPn,r\mathcal{L}yn_{P_{n},r} and 𝒰​𝒯n,r\mathcal{UT}_{n,r} given below. By the discussion in Example 4.10, we can view the trees in ℒ​y​nPn,r\mathcal{L}yn_{P_{n},r} as unlabeled binary trees whose internal nodes are colored with colors in [r][r]. We represent such a binary tree TT as T=TL​∧𝑐​TRT=T_{L}\overset{c}{\land}T_{R}, where TLT_{L} is the colored left subtree of TT, TRT_{R} is the colored right subtree of TT, and cc is the color of the root of TT. Then the (unlabeled) tree T∈ℒ​y​nPn,rT\in\mathcal{L}yn_{P_{n},r} if and only if

T=(…(T0∧c1T1)∧c2⋯)∧ckTk,T=(\dots(T_{0}\overset{c_{1}}{\land}T_{1})\overset{c_{2}}{\land}\cdots)\overset{c_{k}}{\land}T_{k},

where T0T_{0} is a single (unlabeled) leaf, each (unlabeled) Ti∈ℒ​y​nPni,rT_{i}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{P_{n_{i}},r}, for some nin_{i}, and r≥c1>c2>⋯>ck≥1r\geq c_{1}>c_{2}>\dots>c_{k}\geq 1. Now let ψ⁡(T)\psi(T) be the rr-ary tree defined recursively by letting the iith subtree of the root of ψ⁡(T)\psi(T) be ψ⁡(Tj)\psi(T_{j}) if i=cji=c_{j} and be a leaf if i∈[r]−{c1,…,ck}i\in[r]-\{c_{1},\dots,c_{k}\}. This defines a map from ℒ​y​nPn,r\mathcal{L}yn_{P_{n},r} to 𝒰​𝒯n,r\mathcal{UT}_{n,r}, which is easily seen to be a bijection. Also, for each ν∈WCompn,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n,r}, we have T∈ℒ​y​nPn,νT\in\mathcal{L}yn_{P_{n},\nu} if and only if ψ⁡(T)∈𝒰​𝒯ν,r\psi(T)\in\mathcal{UT}_{\nu,r}. Hence |ℒ​y​nPn,ν|=|𝒰​𝒯ν,r||\mathcal{L}yn_{P_{n},\nu}|=|\mathcal{UT}_{\nu,r}|. ∎

Remark 6.23.

Note that Corollary 5.10 and Theorem 6.22 imply that |𝒰​𝒯ν,r||\mathcal{UT}_{\nu,r}| is equal to the generalized Fuss-Narayana number NνN_{\nu} for all ν∈WCompn−1,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r}. This is a refinement of the well known result that the Fuss-Catalan numbers count rr-ary trees.

Remark 6.24.

An alternative proof of Theorem 5.9 can be given that uses Theorem 6.18 and a bijection from 𝒩Pn\mathcal{N}_{P_{n}} to the set of noncrossing partitions 𝒩​𝒞n\mathcal{NC}_{n}. By the discussion in Example 4.10, we can ignore the leaf labels and view the trees in 𝒩Pn\mathcal{N}_{P_{n}} as trees in 𝒰​𝒯n,2\mathcal{UT}_{n,2}. The bijection is as follows. For each T∈𝒰​𝒯n,2T\in\mathcal{UT}_{n,2}, label its internal nodes in inorder (i.e. left subtree labeled in inorder first, then root, then right subtree labeled in inorder) and let π⁡(T)\pi(T) be the partition of [n][n] whose blocks are the maximal left paths of labeled internal nodes of TT, that is, the blocks of π⁡(T)\pi(T) are of the form {x1,…,xm}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{m}\}, where L⁡(xi)=xi+1L(x_{i})=x_{i+1} for all i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1], x1x_{1} is not a left child and the left child of xmx_{m} is a leaf. We leave it to the reader to check that this defines a bijection π:𝒩Pn=𝒰​𝒯n,2→𝒩​𝒞n\pi:\mathcal{N}_{P_{n}}=\mathcal{UT}_{n,2}\to\mathcal{NC}_{n}. Note that the Lyndon type λ⁡(T)\lambda(T) of each T∈𝒩PnT\in\mathcal{N}_{P_{n}} is equal to the block type λ⁡(π⁡(T))\lambda(\pi(T)). Hence π\pi is a bijection from 𝒩Pn\mathcal{N}_{P_{n}} to 𝒩​𝒞n\mathcal{NC}_{n} that takes Lyndon type to block type. Theorem 5.9 now follows from (5.9) and Theorem 6.18.

Next we apply Theorem 6.18 to the star graph S​tnSt_{n}. For each subset S={s1,s2,…,sk−1}<S=\{s_{1},s_{2},\dots,s_{k-1}\}_{<} of [n−1][n-1], the composition of nn associated with SS is defined by,

co(S)=(s1,s2−s1,s3−s2,…,n−sk−1).\mathop{\rm co}\nolimits(S)=(s_{1},s_{2}-s_{1},s_{3}-s_{2},\dots,n-s_{k-1}).

Given a composition ν\nu with kk parts, let eνe_{\nu} be the elementary symmetric function eν⁡(1)eν⁡(2)⋯eν⁡(k)e_{\nu(1)}e_{\nu(2)}\cdots e_{\nu(k)}. Recall, the descent set Des(σ)\mathop{\rm Des}\nolimits(\sigma) of a permutation σ∈𝔖n\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n} is defined to be

Des(σ):={i∈[n−1]:σ⁡(i)>σ⁡(i+1)}.\mathop{\rm Des}\nolimits(\sigma):=\{i\in[n-1]:\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)\}.
Theorem 6.25 ([23]).

For all n≥1n\geq 1,

(−1)n​MS​tn+1​(𝐱)=∑σ∈𝔖neco(Des(σ))​(𝐱).(-1)^{n}M_{St_{n+1}}(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}e_{\mathop{\rm co}\nolimits(\mathop{\rm Des}\nolimits(\sigma))}(\mathbf{x}).

Hence for all T∈𝒩S​tn+1T\in\mathcal{N}_{St_{n+1}}, we have eλ⁡(T)=eco(Des(σT))e_{\lambda(T)}=e_{\mathop{\rm co}\nolimits(\mathop{\rm Des}\nolimits(\sigma_{T}))}. Remark 6.26.

Let Λℚn\Lambda_{\mathbb{Q}}^{n} be the vector space of homogeneous symmetric functions of degree nn over ℚ\mathbb{Q}. Let η:Λℚn→ℚ⁡[t]\eta:\Lambda_{\mathbb{Q}}^{n}\to\mathbb{Q}[t] be the homomorphism defined on the basis {eλ:λ⊢n}\{e_{\lambda}:\lambda\vdash n\} by η⁡(eλ)=tℓ⁡(λ)−1\eta(e_{\lambda})=t^{\ell(\lambda)-1}.

(1) In [22] González D’León shows that (−1)n−1​η​(MKn​(𝐱))(-1)^{n-1}\eta(M_{K_{n}}(\mathbf{x})) is equal to a polynomial whose coefficients are called second order Eulerian numbers in [26]. Stanley and Gessel [19] give a combinatorial interpretation of these polynomials in terms of descent number of certain multiset permutations that they call Stirling permutations. In [24] González D’León gives a combinatorial interpretation of (−1)n−1​MKn​(𝐱)(-1)^{n-1}M_{K_{n}}(\mathbf{x}) in terms of Stirling permutations, which, under the specialization η\eta, reduces to the Stanley-Gessel interpretation of the second order Eulerian polynomials.

(2) It follows from Equation (5.10) and a well-known interpretation of the Narayana polynomials as Nn​(t)=∑π∈𝒩​𝒞nt|π|−1N_{n}(t)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathcal{NC}_{n}}t^{|\pi|-1} that

(−1)n−1​η​(MPn​(𝐱))=Nn−1​(t).(-1)^{n-1}\eta(M_{P_{n}}(\mathbf{x}))=N_{n-1}(t).

(−1)n−1​η​(MS​tn​(𝐱))=An−1​(t),(-1)^{n-1}\eta(M_{St_{n}}(\mathbf{x}))=A_{n-1}(t),

which appeared in [24].

6.5. Topological consequences

Although not needed in the rest of the paper, we discuss some topological consequences of the EL-labeling of Theorem 6.12. First we recall the well-known Philip Hall’s theorem stating that given any open interval (x,y)(x,y) of a pure bounded finite poset PP, the value of the Möbius function μP​(x,y)\mu_{P}(x,y) is equal to the reduced Euler characteristic of the order complex Δ⁡(x,y)\Delta(x,y) of the interval (x,y)(x,y), where the order complex of a poset is the simplicial complex whose faces are the chains of the poset. An EL-labeling has the following further topological and homological implications for the order complex Δ⁡(x,y)\Delta(x,y).

Theorem 6.27 (Björner [9], Björner and Wachs [4, Theorem 5.9], cf. Wachs [46, Theorem 3.2.4]).

Let λ\lambda be an EL-labeling of a pure bounded finite poset PP. Then for each open interval (x,y)(x,y) of PP we have that,

  1. (1)

    the order complex Δ⁡(x,y)\Delta(x,y) has the homotopy type of a wedge of

    |{𝐜∣𝐜​ is an ascent-free maximal chain of ​[x,y]}||\{\mathbf{c}\mid\mathbf{c}\text{ is an ascent-free maximal chain of }[x,y]\}|

    ℓ⁡(x,y)\ell(x,y)-spheres, and hence the poset PP is Cohen-Macaulay, i.e., H~d​(Δ⁡(x,y))=0\widetilde{H}^{d}(\Delta(x,y))=0 for every d≠ℓ⁡(x,y)d\neq\ell(x,y);

  2. (2)

    the set

    {𝐜¯∣𝐜​ is an ascent-free maximal chain of ​[x,y]}\{\bar{\mathbf{c}}\mid\mathbf{c}\text{ is an ascent-free maximal chain of }[x,y]\}

    forms a basis for the reduced cohomology H~ℓ⁡(x,y)​(Δ​(x,y))\widetilde{H}^{\ell(x,y)}(\Delta(x,y)).

The following are therefore topological consequences of Theorems 6.12 and 6.15. These consequences were proved in [22] (r=2r=2 case in [20]) for G=KnG=K_{n}.

Theorem 6.28.

Let GG be a connected chordal graph on [n][n] and let r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}. Then ΠGr^\widehat{\Pi^{r}_{G}} is Cohen-Macaulay.

Theorem 6.29.

Let GG be a connected perfectly labeled chordal graph on [n][n] and let ν∈WCompn−1,r\nu\in{\rm WComp}_{n-1,r}, where r∈ℤ>0∪{∞}r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\cup\{\infty\}. Then the set

{c¯​(𝐓,ρT)∣𝐓∈ℒ​y​nG,ν},\{\bar{c}(\mathbf{T},\rho_{T})\mid\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}\},

where c¯​(𝐓,ρT):=c⁡(𝐓,ρT)∖{0^,[n]ν}\bar{c}(\mathbf{T},\rho_{T}):=c(\mathbf{T},\rho_{T})\setminus\{\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}\} and ρT\rho_{T} is any linear extension of TT, is a basis for top cohomology H~n−3​(Δ⁡(0^,[n]ν))\widetilde{H}^{n-3}(\Delta(\hat{0},[n]^{\nu})) of the order complex Δ⁡(0^,[n]ν)\Delta(\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}) of the open interval (0^,[n]ν)(\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}) of ΠGr\Pi^{r}_{G}.

Proof.

It follows from Theorems 6.27 and 6.15 that

{c¯​(𝐓,τT)∣𝐓∈ℒ​y​nG,ν},\{\bar{c}(\mathbf{T},\tau_{T})\mid\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}\},

where τT\tau_{T} is the decreasing-minimum linear extension, is a basis for top cohomology of the open interval (0^,[n]ν)(\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}). We claim that if τ\tau and τ′\tau^{\prime} are any two linear extensions of the internal nodes of 𝐓∈ℒ​y​nG,ν\mathbf{T}\in\mathcal{L}yn_{G,\nu}, then in the top cohomology group of the order complex of the interval (0^,[n]ν)(\hat{0},[n]^{\nu}) of ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r} we have that

c¯​(𝐓,τ)=±c¯​(𝐓,τ′).\bar{c}(\mathbf{T},\tau)=\pm\bar{c}(\mathbf{T},\tau^{\prime}).

Indeed, this was proved in [22] for G=KnG=K_{n} and the proof goes through for any connected perfectly labeled chordal graph GG. It follows that the decreasing-minimum linear extension τT\tau_{T} can be replaced by any linear extension ρT\rho_{T}. ∎

7. A symmetric function analog of the chromatic polynomial

We consider a symmetric function analog of the characteristic polynomial of a bond lattice. Thanks to Whitney’s formula in Equation (1.4), this is a symmetric function analog of the chromatic polynomial of a graph, which is different from Stanley’s well-known chromatic symmetric function [44].

7.1. Preliminaries

Given a pure (or ranked) poset PP, the characteristic polynomial of a pure poset PP with a minimum element 0^\hat{0} is defined as

chP​(t):=∑x∈PμP​(0^,x)​tρ⁡(x),{\rm ch}_{P}(t):=\sum_{x\in P}\mu_{P}(\hat{0},x)t^{\rho(x)},

where ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) is the rank of xx, i.e., the length of the interval [0^,x][\hat{0},x].

For any graph GG, let

(7.1) ΨG​(𝐱)\displaystyle\Psi_{G}(\mathbf{x}) =∑𝝅∈ΠG∞μΠG∞​(0^,𝝅)​𝐱w⁡(𝝅)\displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{\pi}\in\Pi_{G}^{\infty}}\mu_{\Pi_{G}^{\infty}}(\hat{0},\boldsymbol{\pi})\mathbf{x}^{w(\boldsymbol{\pi})}

Equivalently,

ΨG​(𝐱)\displaystyle\Psi_{G}(\mathbf{x}) =∑π∈ΠGMG|π​(𝐱)\displaystyle=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_{G}}M_{G|_{\pi}}(\mathbf{x})

where G|πG|_{\pi} is the subgraph of GG whose connected components are of the form G|BG|_{B} where B∈πB\in\pi. For example,

(7.2) ΨP3​(𝐱)\displaystyle\Psi_{P_{3}}(\mathbf{x}) =1−2​e1​(𝐱)+e1,1​(𝐱)+e2​(𝐱)\displaystyle=1-2e_{1}(\mathbf{x})+e_{1,1}(\mathbf{x})+e_{2}(\mathbf{x})

The specialization ΨG​(t,t,…,t⏞r,0,0,…)\Psi_{G}(\stackrel{{\scriptstyle r}}{{\overbrace{t,t,\dots,t}}},0,0,\dots) is equal to the characteristic polynomial of the rr-weighted bond poset ΠGr\Pi^{r}_{G}. By (1.4), the chromatic polynomial χG​(t)\chi_{G}(t) is obtained from ΨG​(t,0,0,…)\Psi_{G}(t,0,0,\dots) by reversing its coefficients. That is

ΨG​(t,0,0,…)=tn​χG​(t−1),\Psi_{G}(t,0,0,\dots)=t^{n}\chi_{G}(t^{-1}),

where nn is the number of vertices of GG. Thus we may think of ΨG​(𝐱)\Psi_{G}(\mathbf{x}) as a symmetric function analog of the chromatic polynomial.

There is a well-known classical formula for the characteristic polynomial of ΠKn=Πn\Pi_{K_{n}}=\Pi_{n} given by,

(7.3) ΨKn(t,0,0,0,…)=(t−1)(t−2)⋯(t−n+1).\Psi_{K_{n}}(t,0,0,0,\dots)=(t-1)(t-2)\cdots(t-n+1).

The formula for the characteristic polynomial of ΠKn2=𝒲​ΠKn\Pi^{2}_{K_{n}}=\mathcal{W}\Pi_{K_{n}} was given in [20, Theorem 2.8],

(7.4) ΨKn​(t,t,0,0,…)=(t−n)n−1.\Psi_{K_{n}}(t,t,0,0,\dots)=(t-n)^{n-1}.
Question 7.1.

Are there nice formulas for ΨKn​(t,t,…,t⏞r,0,0,…)\Psi_{K_{n}}(\stackrel{{\scriptstyle r}}{{\overbrace{t,t,\dots,t}}},0,0,\dots) when r>2r>2?

7.2. Alternating ee-positivity and Schur-log-concavity

The next theorem generalizes, in the case of chordal graphs, the fact that the characteristic polynomials of bond lattices alternate in sign. Given a symmetric function f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}), let f⁡(𝐱)|deg⁡df(\mathbf{x})|_{\deg d} denote the degree dd homogeneous component of f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}). We say that f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) is alternating ee-positive if (−1)d​f​(𝐱)|deg⁡d(-1)^{d}f(\mathbf{x})|_{\deg d} is ee-positive for all d≥0d\geq 0.

Theorem 7.2.

If GG is a chordal graph then ΨG​(𝐱)\Psi_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is alternating ee-positive.

Proof.

Let nn be the number of vertices of GG. Note that G|πG|_{\pi} has nn vertices and |π||\pi| connected components for all π∈ΠG\pi\in\Pi_{G}. Since MG|π​(𝐱)M_{G|_{\pi}}(\mathbf{x}) is homogeneous of degree n−|π|n-|\pi|, for all dd we have

ΨG​(𝐱)|deg⁡d=∑π∈ΠG|π|=n−dMG|π​(𝐱).\Psi_{G}(\mathbf{x})|_{\deg d}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\pi\in\Pi_{G}\\ |\pi|=n-d\end{subarray}}M_{G|_{\pi}}(\mathbf{x}).

Since GG is chordal, each G|πG|_{\pi} is chordal. We can therefore apply Corollary 6.19 to each G|πG|_{\pi}. Thus, if |π|=n−d|\pi|=n-d then (−1)d​MG|π​(𝐱)(-1)^{d}M_{G|_{\pi}}(\mathbf{x}) is ee-positive. It follows that each (−1)d​ΨG​(𝐱)|deg⁡d(-1)^{d}\Psi_{G}(\mathbf{x})|_{\deg d} is ee-positive giving the desired result. ∎

A similar argument shows that Conjecture 6.21 (1) is equivalent to the conjecture that Theorem 7.2 is true for any graph.

A polynomial ∑j=0daj​tj∈ℝ⁡[t]\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_{j}t^{j}\in\mathbb{R}[t] is said to be log-concave if for all i∈[d−1]i\in[d-1],

(7.5) ai2≥ai−1​ai+1.a_{i}^{2}\geq a_{i-1}a_{i+1}.

For sequences of positive real numbers, log-concavity implies unimodality (see [10, Lemma 1.1]).

A longstanding conjecture of Hoggar [29], proved in 2012 by Huh [30], asserts that for any graph GG, the chromatic polynomial χG​(t)\chi_{G}(t) is log-concave. Since the coefficients of the chromatic polynomial alternate in sign, Huh’s result also settles a conjecture of Read [36] stating that (−1)n​χG​(−t)(-1)^{n}\chi_{G}(-t) is unimodal.

Note that log-concavity of χG​(t)\chi_{G}(t) is equivalent to log-concavity of ΨG​(t,0,0,…)\Psi_{G}(t,0,0,\dots) since the sequences of coefficients are the reverse of each other. This leads to the following conjectural generalization. We will say that a symmetric function f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}) is Schur-log-concave if for all d≥1d\geq 1,

(f⁡(𝐱)|deg⁡d)2−f⁡(𝐱)|deg⁡d−1​f​(𝐱)|deg⁡d+1(f(\mathbf{x})|_{\deg d})^{2}-f(\mathbf{x})|_{\deg d-1}f(\mathbf{x})|_{\deg d+1}

is Schur-positive (i.e., when expanded in the Schur basis {sλ(𝐱):λ⊢2d}\{s_{\lambda}(\mathbf{x}):\lambda\vdash 2d\}, the coefficients are nonnegative). The following conjecture has been shown computationally for all connected graphs GG with at most 77 vertices.

Conjecture 7.3.

For any graph GG, the symmetric function ΨG​(𝐱)\Psi_{G}(\mathbf{x}) is Schur-log-concave.

Example 7.4.

Checking the Schur-log-concavity condition at d=1d=1 for ΨP3​(𝐱)\Psi_{P_{3}}(\mathbf{x}) from Equation (7.2) yields

(−2​e1​(𝐱))2−(1)​(e1,1​(𝐱)+e2​(𝐱))\displaystyle(-2e_{1}(\mathbf{x}))^{2}-(1)(e_{1,1}(\mathbf{x})+e_{2}(\mathbf{x})) =3​s1,1​(𝐱)+2​s2​(𝐱),\displaystyle=3s_{1,1}(\mathbf{x})+2s_{2}(\mathbf{x}),

which is Schur-positive.

Note that Schur-log-concavity of ΨG​(𝐱)\Psi_{G}(\mathbf{x}) implies log-concavity of the characteristic polynomial ΨG​(t,⋯,t,0,0,…)\Psi_{G}(t,\dotsm,t,0,0,\dots) of ΠGr\Pi_{G}^{r} for all rr. Huh’s result (i.e. the r=1 case) is therefore a specialization of Conjecture 7.3 for ΨG​(𝐱)\Psi_{G}(\mathbf{x}). For r=2r=2 and G=KnG=K_{n}, log-concavity of ΨKn​(t,t,0,0,…)\Psi_{K_{n}}(t,t,0,0,\dots) follows from (7.4) and the fact that real-rooted polynomials with nonnegative coefficients are log-concave (see [10, Lemma 1.1]).

In a follow-up paper, we discuss Conjecture 7.3 further, as well as a related symmetric function generalization of the rank polynomial.
